articles.title: Pope needs no further treatment for lung cancer, his doctors say
articles.summary: Pope Leo will not ‌need any further therapy after undergoing ​lung cancer surgery ​last week, his doctors said in ​a statement released by ‌the Vatican on Wednesday.

image.caption: Pope Leo arrives to hold his first weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square since cancer surgery, at the Vatican, Wednesday. His doctors released a statement saying the Pope will not require further therapy for lung cancer. (Yara Nardi/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Pope Leo will not ‌need any further therapy after undergoing ​lung cancer surgery ​last week, his doctors said in ​a statement released by ‌the Vatican on Wednesday.
Pope Leo was diagnosed with pulmonary adenocarcinoma after part of his lung was removed
Pope Leo will not ‌need any further therapy after undergoing ​lung cancer surgery ​last week, his doctors said in ​a statement ⁠released ⁠by ‌the Vatican on Wednesday.
Histological examination results confirmed a ⁠diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, with the disease ‌remaining localized, the doctors said.
"A subsequent oncological evaluation ​has confirmed ⁠that no further therapy ⁠is required," the ⁠Pope's ⁠lead ​surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and ​his ⁠personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said.

The Pope returned to St. Peter's Square Wednesday, waving to pilgrims and blessing babies from his open-air Popemobile as he held his first general audience at the Vatican since undergoing surgery Oct. 13.
After touring the Square, Leo offered a sermon in Italian. In the only major change from previous occasions, he gave brief greetings afterwards in seven other languages, instead of nine.
South American trip planned

The 71-year-old is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader in decades, but it remains unclear if that trip will go ahead as planned.
His lead surgeon has indicated he believes Leo will be well enough to travel.
"I would say there are no clinical reasons why this visit should not take place," he said in an interview with Vatican News.

articles.title: Canadian government sites among those offline after flaw identified in widely used computer language
articles.summary: Developers behind the PHP programming language released a fix on Wednesday after a security vulnerability was brought to light. The PHP developers urged people to implement the fix as quickly as…

image.caption: A person works on their laptop at a cafe in London, Britain, October 21, 2026. Government websites in Canada and Europe went dark on Wednesday as operators raced to patch two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the most widely used programming languages on the web. (Toby Melville/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New

Developers behind the PHP programming language released a fix on Wednesday after a security vulnerability was brought to light. The PHP developers urged people to implement the fix as quickly as possible, and some governments took sites offline as a precautionary measure.
Developers behind the PHP programming language urging companies to implement a fix quickly
Numerous websites, including Canadian government sites, went offline Wednesday in order to implement a fix after a vulnerability was found in PHP, a widely used programming language.
PHP developers on Wednesday released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities in their software, and encouraged website operators to implement the solution as soon as possible.
"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation said in a news release.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said some federal government websites had been taken offline temporarily as a "precautionary measure," and urged organizations whose websites run on PHP to implement the security update.
"We are taking this situation extremely seriously," Solomon said in a post on social media. "The affected websites will be brought back online as soon as the fixes have been applied."
The websites for the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and Statistics Canada website appeared to be down for a period of time on Wednesday when CBC News attempted to access them.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government site was offline on Wednesday following a newly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerability. Multiple Canadian government sites were down on Wednesday because of the vulnerability. (CBC)
The government sites for Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island were also offline, displaying messages saying the shutdown was due to a global security incident.

PHP is a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for "Personal Home Page." It underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into sites like WordPress, ​Drupal, Joomla and Magento.

items: AI agents tried to hack Library and Archives Canada website, research firm says

blocks.text: When a visitor loads a page that uses PHP, a server running the language assembles the content and sends it to the browser. ⁠It is free, open source software, maintained by volunteers.
The flaw in PHP was discovered using artificial intelligence, Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post.
How AI hacked the Australian government and almost got away with it | About That

The company said the vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade, and that they used multiple large language models to find the vulnerability and validate the patch for the problem while working with OpenAI on discovery and patching. They also co-ordinated with Automattic, AWS, Microsoft and others on the rollout of the patch, so they could give guidance to customers that cannot implement the fix immediately.
PHP runs roughly 75 of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs.

Elsewhere around the world, cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain also urged PHP users to make the fix, while governments in France, the Netherlands and other European countries proactively took their websites offline to make the fix.

articles.title: Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms
articles.summary: Far-right Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel reveals the party's plan to reform the EU. Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in Berlin to talk to developers and investors. DW has more.

image.caption: Weidel said the AfD did not want the European Commission to intrude on people's private decision-making [File photo: July 2025]Image: Andreas Gora/IMAGO

blocks.text: October 21, 2026
Weidel pitches 'three pillars' of EU reform at European Parliament

blocks.caption: Alice Weidel (center) said the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any moreImage: Ann-Krisitn Wenzel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.

"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."

On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."

"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."

This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.

She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."

Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.

Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."
"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.
She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."
While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.

articles.title: Macron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest
articles.summary:
Leaders criticised for spreading misleading information as France prepares for further protests this weekend

Emmanuel Macron has accused Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of…

blocks.text: Emmanuel Macron has accused Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of making “stupid comments” about France’s street unrest for political gain, as the country prepared for more protests this weekend.

Speaking during a visit to Qatar, the French president did not name names but said “manipulation of information” after Saturday’s riots had led to “comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders”.

Asked if he was referring to Donald Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.” The US president has blamed France’s violence on “migrants, jihadists and communists” as he campaigns for his Republican party before midterm elections.

Macron told reporters in Doha that some leaders “in the middle of election campaigns, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic” were “naively spreading narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote”.
They were “using our country for their own political campaigns”, the French president said. “And we don’t need that. We already have difficulties to deal with.”

He said AI-generated images were circulating “depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.”

blocks.caption: Largely peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living descended into violence and looting in cities including Paris and Marseille last weekend. Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPA

blocks.text: The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections next weekend, has also said that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Analysts have dismissed claims that migrants were the main factor in France’s protests.

Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has erupted six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday.

Largely peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living rapidly descended into rampant violence and extensive looting, especially in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges, where the town hall was set on fire and partly destroyed.
Police said that protests would be banned in parts of Paris on Thursday as the city braced for more demonstrations.

The unrest has prompted several countries to issue travel warnings for France and rattled already nervous financial markets, with the yield on the French government’s benchmark 10-year bonds passing 5% on Wednesday, its highest since 2002.

Macron pledged to prevent any repeat of last weekend’s convulsions, as the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) grassroots protest movement formally filed plans for a march through the centre of Paris ⁠on Saturday that is likely to be the ⁠government’s next big test.

Student groups have also called for protests on the same day to push demands for greater investment in education. The gilets jaunes activists aim to revive their nationwide 2018 campaign against rising living costs and declining public services.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The city hall in Limoges was destroyed by fire during the protests last weekend.  Photograph: SDIS 87/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Those who want to cause disorder in city centres next Saturday will be prevented from doing so,” Macron told reporters in the Gulf, where he was seeking energy deals to help offset rising fuel costs. “There must be no wavering at the top of the state.”

Government ministers have promised a “massive” and vastly reinforced security operation after acknowledging shortcomings in their initial response last weekend, with some troops expected to be deployed alongside police reinforcements.

Partial night-time curfews imposed on Monday and Tuesday in areas prone to violent protests and looting in cities around France, including Paris, Marseille and Lille, have helped ensure relative calm and were expected to be renewed on Wednesday.

France’s main trade unions have separately called a nationwide mobilisation for 5 November. Sophie Binet, the head of the CGT union, said: “There is huge and legitimate anger, and the answer to that situation is not repression. It is a political response.”

Macron insisted France “doesn’t need a state of emergency”, saying it “has the means” to control any further unrest. Union representatives met the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on Wednesday but no concrete announcements followed.

Sometimes violent protests in European countries including Italy and Belgium have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading across the continent where with many nations, including France, face budget problems.
Italy’s government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there.

articles.title: NSW passes ‘human compost’ laws with several MPs saying they will utilise practice after they die
articles.summary:
Australia-first laws provide a third legal option other than burial and cremation for the treatment of bodies

  • Get our

blocks.text: Several New South Wales MPs say they want their own bodies turned into “human compost” after Australian-first laws were passed allowing the unusual practice.
The laws, passed on Wednesday, provide a third legal option other than burial and cremation for the treatment of bodies.
The private member’s bill was introduced by independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich, who travelled to Germany and the US to research the practice, which is allowed in some parts of both countries.
The practice, known as natural organic reduction, terramation or human composting, involves placing the body in a temperature-controlled vessel with organic matter such as alfalfa, straw or mulch.
Once inside, the vessel is turned or rocked to circulate air. The introduced matter reacts with the air and feeds the body’s naturally occurring microbes to rapidly decompose the body.

The process creates heat that, after about 30 days, transforms the body into soil. When rested for about 30 days more, the vessel contains about 110kg of “dry, rich soil that is fertile and free of pathogens”, Greenwich told the legislative assembly earlier this year.

In the legislative council on Wednesday, John Ruddick, a Libertarian MP, said he backed what Greens MP Dr Amanda Cohn said in supporting the bill: he thought it was likely he would choose terramation over a burial plot or cremation.
“Terramation will be voluntary. It is a choice. A lot of people may not choose it … I am pretty sure that I will put in my will that I wish to be terramated,” Ruddick said.
“I like the idea of being buried somewhere and having a nice big gum tree grow there for 100 years.
“The idea of being cremated or buried has always freaked me out. This is a much better option.”

blocks.caption: Cameron Murphy says he looks forward to ‘being able to utilise this service in the long-distant future after it becomes law’.  Photograph: Carly Earl/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Labor MP Cameron Murphy also said: “I look forward to being able to utilise this service in the long-distant future after it becomes law”.
Liberal MP Susan Carter urged the government to consider when it implemented the bill how to ensure the dead were respected.
“Terramation should not simply become a human compost bin,” she said.
“Like all the many ways in which we approach death, it should help those who remain to mourn, and the respect shown to that person in life should continue into death.
after newsletter promotion
“It is important for that person, for their family, and for the whole way in which we go forward as a society.”
Emma Hurst MP, the Animal Justice MP who introduced the bill into the legislative council, told parliament on Wednesday that terramation had significant environmental benefits.

She said it could avoid the need for large burial plots and can be wholly carbon neutral, compared with cremation, which she said was energy intensive and released substantial greenhouse gas emissions.
“Terramation provides possibilities to grow living things, like trees and plants, in honour of a life,” Hurst said.

“Because terramation is a slow process, there are multiple opportunities for ceremonies, including for the laying of the body in the vessel and for opening the vessel after a body has been terramated.
“Facilities overseas have allowed families to visit during the terramation process. It is a natural and gentle process that, for some, can help with grieving.”
The bill passed on Wednesday gives the NSW government 18 months to create regulations to control the practice, which would be limited to specialised facilities.

articles.title: Trump, Putin and Xi at one table, without Ukraine. What Moscow wants from the proposal and why Beijing might agree.
articles.summary: Moscow is pushing for a summit with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, without Kyiv or the EU. What does Russia hope to gain, and why might China be willing to take…
articles.byline: Asja Lokina, Roman Goncharenko, Ismi Aghayev

image.caption: What's in it for China if it mediates between Russia and the US?Image: Kristina Solovyova/Sputnik/REUTERS

blocks.text: The administration of US President Donald Trump has stepped up diplomatic efforts this autumn to revive stalled negotiations aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine.

Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv and its European partners while seeking to draw Moscow back to the negotiating table through a series of concessions, including a deal involving Russian diesel exports to the US and the temporary easing of some sanctions.

Yet the Kremlin appears in no hurry to resume meaningful peace talks. Moscow is ready to hold negotiations with Ukraine at a technical level next month, the Kremlin said after the meeting between US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on November 21.

Putin agreed to resume the peace talks mediated by Washington after November 10, his aide Yury Ushakov said after the meeting. He added that the next round of negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi and would focus on "building the security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the war."

blocks.caption: US special envoy Steve Witkoff at and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands during a meeting in St. Petersburg on October 21Image: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/REUTERS

blocks.text: According to his aide, Putin also shared some thoughts with Witkoff on the possible trilateral summit involving US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Ushakov pointed out that Beijing is already preparing the meeting.
Trilateral summit in China without Ukraine

Moscow proposed to hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen, China, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week. According to WSJ sources, Putin hopes to reach an agreement with Trump and Xi on ending the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Russia.

Moscow's proposal for the three-way summit involving Russia, the United States and China — but excluding Ukraine and the European Union — offers a glimpse of the negotiating format the Kremlin would prefer. Russia insists that Ukraine must be prepared to make territorial concessions before negotiations can move forward. Putin has also repeatedly stressed that he is willing to negotiate only if Russian interests are taken into account.

According to the WSJ, Putin views the proposed gathering in Shenzhen as a potential new Yalta Conference, referring to the 1945 meeting of the leaders of the United States, Great Britain and the Soviet Union to discuss the defeat of Nazi Germany and the postwar order in Europe.

The newspaper reported that Chinese officials had indicated through diplomatic channels that Beijing would not object to the three-way format if Trump agreed to participate. Trump, whose relations with Kyiv have deteriorated significantly in recent weeks, has also expressed openness to such talks.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pointed out during his visit in Oslo on October 20 that talks concerning the future of his country will be acceptable only if Ukraine gets a seat at the negotiating table.
What does China stand to gain from the talks?

Temur Umarov, a researcher at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin who specializes in China-Russia relations, is not surprised by the Kremlin's proposal. He told DW that Moscow wants to feel respected by Washington and treated as a major international power.

The previous US administration was unwilling to discuss questions affecting Ukraine's sovereignty with Russia without Kyiv's participation. Now, Umarov said, the Kremlin believes such negotiations may have become possible.

Moscow apparently hopes that any agreement reached at the proposed meeting would prompt the White House to pressure Ukraine and the EU into accepting its terms. But what role would China actually play?

Umarov believes Beijing would participate largely as a symbolic partner, rather than as an active mediator responsible for the outcome. "Beijing has no intention of taking responsibility for Ukraine's future," he said.

blocks.caption: China's leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump agreed to hold a trilateral summit with Russia in ShenzhenImage: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Simply attending the summit would not impose any additional obligations on China. "It is hardly surprising that the Kremlin insists on this format," Umarov explained. "Russia wants to demonstrate that it is on an equal footing not only with the United States, but also with China. Yet, objectively speaking, Moscow is not the senior partner in that relationship."

Umarov believes China has little direct interest in such negotiations. Even if the leaders issued a joint statement, Beijing would seek language that was as vague and noncommittal as possible, he said. That would allow China to present almost any subsequent development in the war as consistent with the understanding reached at the summit. For Umarov, such flexibility would be essential to Beijing's participation.

However, Yurii Poita, a senior associate researcher at the Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), offers a different assessment. He believes China and Russia have overlapping strategic interests, particularly in their efforts to promote an alternative security architecture across Eurasia.

Both countries, he argues, would benefit from a reduction in Western military presence in Europe and Asia and from a weakening of NATO's influence. "If Russia and China manage to convince the United States to reduce its military presence in Europe and military assistance to Ukraine, Russia would gain additional advantages on the battlefield," Poita told DW.

He added that such a development would further undermine the EU's confidence in the United States as a NATO ally. Poita believes Moscow and Beijing would seek precisely these outcomes in any negotiations with Washington.
Is Putin's political survival crucial for China?
Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, also doubts that Beijing is preparing to take a more active diplomatic role in ending the war.

Speaking to DW, Kimmage said China may see the conflict as destabilizing and would prefer to maintain trade relations with Ukraine and other countries in the region. But he believes another priority outweighs those concerns. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin," he said.

blocks.caption: President Zelenskyy said deciding on Ukraine's future without Ukraine was unacceptableImage: Dan Bashakov/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to Kimmage, Russia provides China with several geopolitical advantages, including low-cost energy and a foreign policy partner that rarely stands in Beijing's way.

He believes China will continue indirectly supporting Russia's military efforts to prevent a Russian defeat. An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said, but ensuring Putin does not lose is crucial. For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.
Does excluding Europe reveal the EU's weakness?
Neither Ukraine nor the European Union would be part of the proposed talks in China.
Kateryna Krasina, a junior researcher at the Kyiv-based New Geopolitics Network, believes their exclusion could reveal how Beijing actually views their international influence.
In her assessment, China's approach suggests that it does not regard Ukraine as an independent player in the negotiations and considers Europe relatively weak.
Kimmage, however, argues that excluding Europe from the summit would not necessarily diminish its influence over the course of the negotiations.

He acknowledged that European governments may have little power to prevent a meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi. But he pointed to European efforts surrounding the 2025 Alaska summit between Trump and Putin, which he believes helped prevent outcomes that would have been unfavorable to Europe.
Kimmage said Europe's influence has grown through financial assistance to Ukraine and extensive defense industry cooperation, particularly involving Germany and other European countries.
He argued that European support has played an important role in Ukraine's ability to resist Russian advances. "And that support equals leverage," Kimmage said.
He believes Russia, China and the United States may all be interested in portraying Europe as a secondary power, but that such a portrayal would overlook Europe's actual influence.

"The optics and the reality are not quite the same," he said, drawing a distinction between the appearance of great-power diplomacy resembling the Yalta Conference and Europe's role in supporting Ukraine.
Umarov offers another perspective.
He believes that any diplomatic agreement between the US, Russia and China would face the reality on the ground.
"China understands that whatever the outcome of negotiations with the United States and Russia, the reality on the ground will be very different and will depend above all on Ukraine," he said.

"Whether the Kremlin likes it or not, Ukraine has agency of its own. Neither the United States nor Western countries can fully determine what happens on the battlefield through diplomatic pressure alone."
This article was originally published in Russian.

articles.title: Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say
articles.summary: The wife of a diplomat based in Abuja travelled to Kampala for a vacation.

blocks.text: Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for a holiday, the head of Africa's health agency has told the BBC.

The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, where she fell ill three days after arriving home in the Nigerian capital on 3 October, according to Dr Jean Kaseya from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.
Nigeria's health minister has confirmed to the BBC the 42-year-old patient spent two and a half weeks in Kampala, adding that she also made a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return.
"She's stable, she's improving," Muhammad Ali Pate said.
The authorities were working to prevent the virus from spreading and had identified 44 people who had been in contact with the woman, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, the minister said.
"Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible," Pate told the BBC.

None of the contacts, who are now in isolation, are known to have developed symptoms, including the person the patient travelled with, the health minister said, adding that the woman had not travelled outside Abuja since landing.
Kaseya explained that the woman had first developed symptoms on 6 October when she had sought medical help.

"She went to the first hospital, a private hospital, thinking that she had malaria, and then she went to the second private hospital. She was admitted on the 11th," he told the BBC's Newshour programme.
Malaria is endemic in Nigeria and its symptoms - a high temperature, headaches, muscle aches, vomiting and or diarrhoea - are similar to those of Ebola.
After her condition failed to improve, public health authorities were alerted on Monday 19 October, Pate said.
Her diagnosis was confirmed the next day following three laboratory tests, he said.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external.
Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.
There have been conflicting accounts about the patient in Nigeria and her movements.

Pate and Kaseya's comments contradict a statement issued earlier by the Ugandan ministry of health, which described the woman as a Nigerian national who had gone to eastern DR Congo for business, only transiting through Uganda.
It insisted there were currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country and that the woman's passage through Uganda did not mean she had contracted the virus there.
Nigeria's health minister and the Africa CDC chief have sought to play down any tension.
Pate said Nigerian officials were working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the full facts.
"We respect our sister nation of Uganda," he said. "We have very strong solidarity, we are all in it together."
Kaseya also urged African countries to share information, saying this would help investigators trace the woman's movements and establish where she might have contracted the virus.
And he encouraged Western countries not to impose travel restrictions, saying "collaboration and solidarity" were the way to help stop the current outbreak.
The disease recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.
On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.
In 2014, Nigeria successfully contained an Ebola outbreak, which had resulted in 20 confirmed cases and eight deaths.
Pate expressed confidence in the country's ability to repeat that success, citing strengthened disease surveillance, laboratories and thousands of trained epidemiologists.
"Nigeria has muscle memory that has been activated, but we are not fighting the past outbreak in the exactly the same way. We have to be vigilant," he said.
The outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Additional reporting by Timothy Obiezu and Lucy Fleming

articles.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in Cambridge Analytica case
articles.summary: A New Mexico judge ordered Facebook's parent company, Meta, to pay $25 billion for misleading users over the Cambridge Analytica breach, which took place during Donald Trump's first presidential…

image.caption: Meta has faced multiple legal challenges over its record on privacy, content moderation, and effects on minorsImage: Andre M. Chang/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: US tech giant Meta, owner of Facebook, was ordered to pay $25 billion (around €22.5 billion) to the US state of New Mexico after a jury found Facebook deceived its users over privacy and content moderation.
"Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false," Judge ⁠Francis ⁠Mathew wrote in his order following the Wednesday verdict.

The case links back to the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal, when a third-party quiz harvested the data of some 87 million Facebook profiles and sold it to the UK-based political consulting firm. The firm used the data for targeted ads, including campaign ads for Donald Trump's first presidential run.
New Mexico rejects deal with Meta

Nearly all US states agreed to settle with Facebook over a myriad of legal issues for an overall payment of $18 billion in August. This included releasing the company from future liability for the Cambridge Analytica breach.
Meta settles for $18B. What it means for you.

New Mexico refused to settle and filed a lawsuit against the platform. Prosecutors claimed that the social network deceived the state's entire population of some 2.1 million people by its public statements on privacy. The US state also argued that Facebook allowed the spread of misinformation and violent content.
In turn, the company's lawyers said the state failed to prove people were actually harmed by Facebook's statements, and claimed the platform had robust content moderation.
In September, a jury found Facebook liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws. Meta pledged to "continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record."
Meta's billions could go to New Mexico's education system

Following the jury's decision last month, it was up to the court to determine how much Meta would pay the state. While the $25 billion fine is lower than the $35 billion to $40 billion demanded by the New Mexico prosecutors, it far exceeds the cap of $3.45 billion suggested by Meta's lawyers.
US jury fines Meta in landmark child‑safety case
"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is ​money, and the value of its stock price," New Mexico attorney Randi McGinn said during the trial.
On Wednesday, New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said the outcome should be "an unambiguous message" to Silicon Valley.
While noting that the money will likely be tied up due to appeals, Torrez also noted that the fine is legally due to be paid into New Mexico's education fund.
"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," he said.

The case is the latest in the string of legal challenges large social media companies face in the US and other parts of the world, including the separate August verdict in New Mexico ordering Facebook to pay $567 million over harm to children.

articles.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
articles.summary: The fine is the largest to date against Facebook's owner, larger than an $18bn deal with California.

blocks.text: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.

A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.
"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices."
Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico." The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.
The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.
New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

That firm utilized data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.
The US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 levied a $5bn fine against the company over its data privacy practices.

Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.

They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly 2 million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said Wednesday.
"Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."
The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional.
Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.
He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years," stretching from 2010 to 2021.
Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public," Judge Mathew wrote in his order.
While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.
A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.
The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children."
California and several other states had collectively sued Meta over similar issues related to a lack of child safety features on Meta's platforms and resulting harms to children.
Meta and the states reached a mutual settlement deal, which did not include a fine or any admission of wrongdoing, to end that case only a few days into what was expected to be a multi-week trial.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s Super Pac spends $500,000 to back New York Republican in midterms
articles.summary: Incumbent Mike Lawler is fending off a challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in state’s 17th congressional district

blocks.text: Elon Musk’s Super Pac has spent more than $500,000 in New York’s highly competitive 17th congressional district race to help Mike Lawler, the Republican incumbent, hold on to his seat.

Lawler, a moderate Republican, is fending off a challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in the Hudson valley. It is among the most-watched races that could determine whether Republicans hold on to their majority in Congress.
America Pac, the Super Pac founded by Musk, has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars over the last year to boost Lawler’s campaign, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
Most of that spending has funded voter outreach efforts such as texting, printing, and postage and digital media-related services. Gothamist was the first to report on Musk’s spending.

Musk, the Republicans’ largest donor so far this midterm cycle, has spent millions of dollars on conservative candidates. Since the beginning of July, Musk has funneled $276m into Republican groups and America Pac, the New York Times reported earlier this month.

The funding is helping push Republican candidates to the finish line as they try to convince disgruntled voters to back the conservative party again. Polling shows Republican candidates are at a slight disadvantage this cycle because many have grown frustrated with the cost of living under Donald Trump.
America Pac’s spending on Lawler’s race is notable because Musk’s Pac spent more than $2m to help re-elect Lawler in 2024.

Conley, Lawler’s Democratic opponent, and the former head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has accused Lawler of protecting Musk rather than regulating artificial intelligence.
after newsletter promotion

“AI poses a very real threat to the safety and security of the American people, and it’s long past time that Congress took action to regulate it,” Conley wrote on X. “But Mike Lawler is standing in the way, because he’s looking out for his trillionaire backer Elon Musk.”

Ciro Riccardi, Lawler’s campaign manager, told Gothamist that they had “no say over what America PAC or any other outside group spends in this race” – referencing a law that prohibits campaigns from coordinating directly with Super Pacs.

articles.title: Judge orders Meta to pay $25B US for misleading consumers about data privacy
articles.summary: Facebook parent company Meta has been ordered to pay $25 billion US after a jury found it misled consumers about data privacy.

image.caption: A Meta logo is shown on a video screen at LlamaCon 2025, an AI developer conference, in Menlo Park, Calif., on April 29, 2025. (Jeff Chiu/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Facebook parent company Meta has been ordered to pay $25 billion US after a jury found it misled consumers about data privacy.
The New Mexico judge found that a penalty of more than $219 billion US was warranted, but reduced it

A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion US (about $35 billion Cdn) on Wednesday after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from ‌millions of Facebook users without their consent.

"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion US was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion US.
A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Kids react to the new restrictions coming to Meta in the U.S.

The state's attorney general sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.

items: Facebook's Cambridge Analytica problem hurts other developers

blocks.text: The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies. The company knew that third parties had broad access to users' personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line, the state said.
Resident misled about privacy

Jurors on Sept. 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.

State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 US ($7,024 Cdn) per violation, with the money directed to New Mexico's school system, New Mexico ⁠Attorney General Raúl Torrez told reporters after the verdict.
Meta agrees to $16.7B US settlement over social media harms to children

At a hearing on Oct. 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, asked Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion US ($49 billion to $56 billion Cdn) saying that would be supported by the U.S. Constitution's protections on due process and the jury's verdict.
"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price," McGinn said.

items: Landmark verdict in New Mexico finds Meta violated state child safety laws

blocks.text: In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion US, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state. The company also said that the evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled.
Two juries sided with state
The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms.

In the first trial, which ended in March, a Santa Fe jury ​found Meta misled users ⁠about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms, and ordered the company to pay $375 million US ($526 million Cdn) in civil penalties. After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567 million US ($796 million Cdn) into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico.

articles.title: Fears of a pan-African Ebola crisis growing as fourth country reports first case
articles.summary: As Nigeria reports its first case of Ebola, fears are growing that the epidemic that started in the Democratic Republic of Congo in May could be on the verge of becoming a bigger regional crisis.

image.caption: Travellers sanitize their hands near a crossing between Kenya and Uganda on Oct. 8. Earlier this month, Kenya reported its first Ebola case, involving a traveller who arrived from Congo via Uganda. (James Keyi/Reuters)

blocks.text: Health·New
As Nigeria reports its first case of Ebola, fears are growing that the epidemic that started in the Democratic Republic of Congo in May could be on the verge of becoming a bigger regional crisis.
Nigeria reported its first case of Ebola on Tuesday, following cases reported in Kenya and Uganda

The epidemic is expanding faster than any previous Ebola outbreak, according to health officials, and has already become the deadliest in Congo's history, with more than 9,500 cases and 4,600 deaths reported as of Sunday.
Nigeria is the fourth African country to detect Ebola since the outbreak began, and is one of three countries with active cases.

"My concern, now that this has spread from East Africa to West Africa, is that we now have a pan-African event, as opposed to a few at-risk countries," said Ayoade Alakija, a Nigerian physician who co-chairs a G7 committee for investment in global health, Reuters reported Wednesday.

The Nigerian case concerns a Ugandan woman who arrived in Nigeria's capital Abuja on Oct. 5, authorities said Wednesday. She had previously travelled in Congo and Uganda, according to Ugandan authorities.

items: Nigeria confirms case of Ebola in capital city of Abuja

blocks.text: Alakija noted that it had taken 12 days since the woman fell sick for her to be tested for Ebola, potentially exposing many other people to the infection.
"Abuja is one of Africa's main cities ... with air and road connections daily, multiple, across the world. It’s a very different prospect — and that's what worries me — the amount of time it took."
Children bear brunt of DRC’s Ebola outbreak
So far, authorities have identified 44 contacts, most of them health-care workers. Health authorities have stated the woman is in isolation.

"This is serious. The virus is spreading across borders and now affects three regions of our continent," Jean Kaseya, director general of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), said on X on Wednesday.

He linked to a statement by Nigeria's health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, in which Pate noted that Nigeria had successfully contained Ebola in 2014, and said they were confident they could do it again.

Members of an Ebola mitigation team disinfect a wooden coffin before loading the body of an unidentified man, who according to his family, died of Ebola, in Bunia, Democratic Republic of Congo, on July 10. (Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters)
"Africa has faced Ebola before, and Africa will defeat it again," Kaseya wrote.
Africa CDC announced Wednesday it will be convening a virtual crisis summit between African health ministers next week to discuss cross-border management of the increasing threat.
Where else has the virus spread?

Earlier this month, Kenya reported its first Ebola case, involving a traveller who arrived from Congo via Uganda. The country has since reported nine cases, all linked to the same patient, who later died of the virus. Authorities have tightened health surveillance at the border in the wake of the cases.

items: 1 in 4 Ebola deaths are children in Democratic Republic of Congo's worst outbreak
Kenya confirms 2nd case of Ebola in relative of patient who died earlier this month
Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo: What's going on and why is the outbreak so alarming?

blocks.text: Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August. Two people died during their outbreak.

Members of the Kenya Red Cross response team direct travellers at the Malaba crossing-point between Kenya and Uganda on Oct. 8 after a man who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled and died of Ebola in Kenya. (Jackson Adika/Reuters)
One case was reported in France in June after a medical doctor returned from the Congo, but no cases have been reported there since.
Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa. With over 240 million people, the West African nation has more than double the amount of people in D.R.C.
The United Nations announced last week that they were scaling up Ebola readiness in 22 countries to be prepared for a greater outbreak.
What makes this strain so transmissible?
This current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare strain that causes Ebola.
There has been two previous outbreaks of Bundibugyo virus in 2007 and 2012, with fatality rates ranging from around 30-50 per cent, but both outbreaks ended with under 100 deaths.

Although its fatality rate isn't generally as high as the Zaire strain of Ebola, which was behind the most widespread Ebola epidemic in history in 2014 in West Africa, causing more than 11,000 deaths, the Bundibugyo virus is so new, and its previous outbreaks so small, that it has no approved treatment or vaccine.

The first cases of the Zaire strain of Ebola were identified in 1976, and it's been the focus of decades of study, with two FDA-approved monoclonal antibody treatments and a vaccine designed to treat it.

Africa CDC is deploying that vaccine to frontline health-care workers while separately studying if it provides some protection against the Bundibugyo virus. Clinical trials are also underway for treatment aimed at Bundibugyo virus, but in the meantime, the lack of treatment is allowing for greater spread.

Health workers and humanitarian responders on the front lines of the Ebola response gather to receive a vaccination in the North Kivu province of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Oct. 16. (Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters)

As the virus is transmitted through contact with the bodily fluids of those who are infected, WHO warns that direct handling of the bodies of those who died of the virus carries a strong risk of transmission.

Health experts have flagged that many in the Congo are avoiding hospitals out of fears that they could catch the virus there, leading to more patients dying in their own homes and then being buried by family members who might not know how to limit their own risks of transmission in the process.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

blocks.text: The CJP is not a registered political party, but a collective which began by mobilising thousands of young people to protest over leaked exam papers.
By July it had emerged as a major force.

A march towards parliament that month ended in clashes with police, drawing wider attention to the movement and increasing pressure on the government. The unrest eventually led to the resignation of India's education minister.
The CJP has since shifted its focus to India's electoral system.

Along with opposition parties, students and other critics of the government, it accuses Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar of revising electoral rolls, an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the allegation.
The SIR exercise has resulted in around 130 million names being removed from voter lists since last year.

Critics warn that the process could also exclude eligible voters, potentially denying them their right to vote, while the Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove ineligible, dead and duplicate entries.

articles.title: Want to book with Air Canada by phone? That'll be an extra $30 please
articles.summary: Air Canada customers who book their flights by phone are now paying $30 per passenger for the privilege.

image.caption: Air Canada has started charging a $30 fee per passenger for booking a flight by phone. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Air Canada customers who book their flights by phone are now paying $30 per passenger for the privilege.
Airline says fee brings it in line with other airlines, including WestJet

The country's largest airline says the policy came into force on Oct. 15, placing it alongside WestJet, United Airlines and the numerous low-cost carriers that charge non-refundable phone booking fees.
Other competitors such as Delta Air Lines and Southwest Airlines still offer tickets by telephone without the surcharge.
For a family of four who books their Air Canada trip the old-fashioned way, the bill will run an extra $120.
The move marks an attempt to steer customers to the company's website or app and to cut call centre costs, or at least compensate for them.

items: Air Canada will now allow you up to 3 mobility aids on flights in expanded policy
WestJet ordered to scrap weight cap on power wheelchairs

blocks.text: "It's expensive. But then again, it's expensive to hire an employee, train them and have them answer the phone," said Andrew D'Amours, co-founder of flight deal site Flytrippers.
The change could disproportionately hit seniors who rely on phone bookings, he said.
"A lot of people, probably older folks, don't really like booking on the app or on the internet. So I get the argument that it's kind of unfair for them."
Trend of 'unbundling' of airline costs

The move also highlights yet another area that airlines have found to charge for services, part of a decade-long trend of "unbundling," where airline customers pay for perks that were once bundled into a standard flight. Passengers now routinely pay extra for checked bags, pre-selected seats, priority boarding and onboard snacks.
Airlines have argued that unbundling allows customers to know precisely what they are paying for, with the cost of a particular service borne more by those who use it.
D'Amours served up a pungent analogy. "If you buy cheese, you can buy the brick and it's much cheaper. Or you can buy it shredded," he said.
"It's more expensive, but you choose that for the convenience. If you don't want to book online, you can pay someone to do it."
Customers who require specialized support, including those with accessibility needs, are exempt from the fee, Air Canada said.
"There is also no change to the support available to you, and no booking fee will apply if your trip is affected by a delay, cancellation or other travel disruption," the company said.
