blocks.text: Russia releases retired school teacher Stephen Hubbard

blocks.caption: Stephen Hubbard in a glass cage in the Moscow City court in Moscow, Russia, Oct. 7, 2024. Photograph: Moscow City Court Press Service/AP

blocks.text: Witkoff announced this morning that Russia authorities had freed Hubbard, the first American known to be convicted of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.

Hubbard, who grew up in Michigan, had been living with his Ukrainian wife in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum. He was arrested when the Russians briefly took over the city at the start of the war in 2022.

In 2024, he was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison by a Russian court. But he has always denied being involved with any combat or military unit, saying that the Russians just took him from his house.
Trump yesterday had flagged Hubbard’s release saying he’d spoken with Putin in regards to the 74-year-old. “It’s time to have Mr Hubbard back,” he said.
Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our coverage of US politics. With 14 days until the mid-terms, we’re heading into the final straight.
President Donald Trump attended a rally last night in North Carolina, where Democrat Roy Cooper is leading Trump’s pick Michael Whatley by a considerable margin.
Undaunted though, Trump said the pollsters “never poll us right” and he predicted “some amazing results”. He’s got another rally in South Carolina later Wednesday.

Overnight he’s also posted on data centers – saying that companies building the energy-intensive sites should pay a “dividend” to the communities where they’re located, including several proposed warehouses in Michigan, where the president will head to on the weekend.

blocks.caption: Trump at a campaign rally at Pitt-Greenville Airport in Greenville, North Carolina, on Tuesday night. Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Trump has been pushing rapid AI expansion but in a nod to how unpopular these water and electricity-guzzling centres are with locals who have to live near them, he’s been hinting at community benefits.
Trump said the “new and giant” centers “are mandated by me to make their own electricity , and ‌give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid”.

Meanwhile US envoy Steve Witkoff is in St Petersburg for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Ukraine; some earlier wrangling by Trump has succeeded in the release of US schoolteacher Stephen Hubbard, who was captured by the Russians and accused of having fought for Ukraine.
Stay with us for all the day’s developments.

articles.title: ASEAN declaration aims for safe, fair recruitment of migrant workers --DMW
articles.summary: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is crafting a declaration that calls for stronger regional action against fraudulent online recruitment and safer migration amid the prevalence of…

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 6:37pm

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is crafting a declaration that calls for stronger regional action against fraudulent online recruitment and safer migration amid the prevalence of human trafficking across the region, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said Wednesday.

The Declaration on the Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Migrant Workers (ACMW) provides an operational framework for member states to address emerging challenges like cyber-enabled recruitment fraud, safe migration pathways, and worker protection guidelines.
"Very relevant sa atin [dahil] may cases ng scam hubs [na biktima] ang mga kabayan natin," DMW Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said during the Kapihan sa Manila Bay forum.
(The declaration is very relevant because we have cases of scam hubs that victimized our countrymen.)
According to Cacdac, the government has so far repatriated 3,000 Filipino victims of scam hubs, some of whom are victims of sex trafficking.
"May law enforcement effort dito ang ASEAN member states to curb itong mga scam hubs, scam farms na tinatawag," Cacdac said.
(The ASEAN member states have law enforcement efforts to curb the scam hubs and scam farms.)
The DMW secretary attributed the prevalence of human trafficking in ASEAN countries to the visa-free jurisdiction in the region.
"Malamang sa malamang itatawid 'yan sa isang visa-free jurisdiction, dun muna sila dadalhin. And then from there, isasakay na sila sa mga fishing boats," Cacdac said.
(Victims are most likely to traverse a visa-free country, then will sail in a fishing boat to their destination.)
With this scheme, ASEAN member states strenghtened it coordination and tighten its borders security.
"On the same page, ang mga ASEAN member states ay magkakaroon ng pagkakaintindihan na ipagbawal ang illegal recruitment," Cacdac said.
(The ASEAN member states are on the same page in prohibiting illegal recruitment.)
"That is why we have tight coordination across ASEAN and within our country with law enforcement," he added.

The Philippines, through DMW, led the 19th ASEAN Forum on Migrant Labour (AFML) this month, where member states discussed the growing threat of cyber-enabled recruitment schemes and how to address it. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Pakistan-Taliban conflict: How India could benefit from shifting regional dynamics
articles.summary: As Pakistan's influence in Afghanistan comes under strain, India is rebuilding ties with the Taliban in Kabul. Can New Delhi turn this diplomatic opening into lasting strategic gains?

image.caption: Clashes between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban erupted in early 2026 [FILE: March 19, 2026]Image: Abdul Basit/AFP

blocks.text: Pakistan and Afghanistan right now are locked in a cycle of escalating tension. Repeated border clashes have strained ties between Islamabad and Kabul.

The current round of tensions began in February 2026, when Pakistan launched strikes into Afghanistan targeting Taliban militants. At one point in March, Pakistan's defense minister said the country was at "open war" with Afghanistan. Periodic bouts of violence have continued since then, with the latest Pakistani strikes targeting the Afghan Taliban's "terrorist hubs" reported earlier in October.

At the heart of the dispute is Pakistan's accusation that the Taliban authorities in Kabul allow the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group, to target Pakistan from Afghan territory. Kabul denies providing the group with sanctuary.
Militants kill dozens of security officers in Pakistan
Where does India come into play?

As the two neighbors trade strikes, the escalating conflict "presents a significant diplomatic and strategic opportunity for India," Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, an Afghanistan expert and founder of the India-based Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.
D'Souza argues the confrontation has weakened Pakistan's traditional influence in Kabul and encouraged the Taliban to broaden its external relations.

"India can respond by expanding diplomatic engagement, humanitarian assistance, development projects and trade, while seeking assurances that Afghan territory will not be used by anti-India militant groups," she said.
However, D'Souza cautioned against interpreting the opening as a fundamental realignment.

"There is no ideological alignment between India and the Taliban," she said. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is likely to pursue a diversified foreign policy rather than align exclusively with New Delhi.

India also lacks the geographical advantages, economic leverage and security presence needed to replace Pakistan's influence, she notes. "The scenario of the Taliban becoming a strategic ally remains far-fetched."
Former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan Amar Sinha warned against viewing the conflict simply as an opportunity for New Delhi to gain at Pakistan's expense.

"The issues have very little to do with India," Sinha told DW, arguing that India was not seeking strategic advantage from the fighting. He also pointed to the consequences of Pakistan's military actions for Afghan civilians.
"Yet the rupture has made Kabul's search for alternative partners more pressing," he added.

For New Delhi, that creates an opening, but not necessarily a strategic alignment, Sinha notes. The Taliban can seek Indian assistance while maintaining relations with China, Russia, Iran and Gulf states, preserving its autonomy rather than exchanging dependence on Pakistan for dependence on India.
The cost of closer ties

Gautam Mukhopadhyaya, another former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan, sees the deterioration in relations between Pakistan and the Taliban as an opportunity for India to recover some of the strategic ground it lost when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
"The crisis has allowed strategic openings for India," Mukhopadhyaya told DW, warning that New Delhi's own treatment of Afghans could undermine its efforts to build a durable relationship.
He pointed to restrictions affecting Afghans seeking Indian visas for education, scholarships, work and medical treatment.
"For all practical purposes, India's security establishment treats Afghans as proxy Pakistanis and 'terrorists' by default," he said.
Former Afghan partners had been left "disappointed, even bitter," Mukhopadhyaya added. "A strategic relationship built on the sands of oppression is not a sound foundation."
'Don't send us back': Afghan women in India fear deportation
Trade cannot overcome geography
India has restored air freight links between Kabul and Delhi and between Kabul and Amritsar in December 2025.
Bilateral trade between India and Afghanistan stood at about $908 million in the 2025-26 fiscal year, while trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan fell sharply amid repeated border closures.

On October 14, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi stressed the importance of relations with India during talks with Indian charge d'affaires Yatin Patel, signaling Kabul's interest in expanding economic cooperation.
But air freight is expensive, and India cannot easily replace Pakistan as a transit route.
New Delhi has sought to use Iran's Chabahar port to improve access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, but regional instability and complications surrounding Iran have constrained those ambitions.
D'Souza cautioned that "the ongoing conflict in Iran" limits India's ability to use Chabahar as a crucial trade and connectivity hub.
Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University specializing in Afghanistan and Eurasian connectivity, highlighted similar obstacles.

"In the last few decades, Islamabad has obstructed Kabul's efforts to gain access to the vast Indian market. However, political instability in Afghanistan and sanctions on Iran have undermined these efforts," Sachdeva told DW.
"Afghanistan's potential as a connector between regional markets remains considerable, but the infrastructure and political conditions needed to realize it are far from assured," he added.

Sachdeva also sees Russia and China as better positioned to shape Afghanistan's wider economic integration. Alternative routes may become more attractive to India, but they are not commercially viable overnight.
Islamabad's security fears

Pakistan has portrayed arch-rival India's growing engagement with the Taliban as a security threat. On October 7, Pakistani diplomat Muhammad Jawad Ajmal accused India at the United Nations of providing the Taliban with material and logistical support.
"Under the guise of humanitarian aid, they have been actively supporting the Taliban regime with material and logistical support for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan," Ajmal said.
The allegation reflects Islamabad's position and has not been established as fact.
Pakistan has accused India of supporting the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army, a militant organization.
India rejects accusations of backing militant activity, while the Taliban denies allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, offered a more nuanced assessment of Pakistan's position.
"India has stepped into a space and is trying to exert its influence and feed anti-Pakistan groups intelligence," she told DW.
Siddiqa added that Pakistan's establishment continues to view the crisis through "a singular security lens."
"Islamabad feels physically squeezed from both sides," she said, adding that closer Kabul-New Delhi ties could create "a dangerous two-front security trap" for Pakistan.
India may gain more room to operate in Afghanistan as ties between Kabul and Islamabad deteriorate. But the Taliban is unlikely to put all its eggs in New Delhi's basket.
Why Pakistan is fighting the Taliban it once backed

articles.title: Government trying to take VP Sara down? Palace calls claim laughable
articles.summary: The Palace on Wednesday thumbed down Vice President Sara Duterte"s claim that the government had a strategy to take her down.

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 6:34pm
The Palace on Wednesday thumbed down Vice President Sara Duterte’s claim that the government had a strategy to take her down.
Duterte earlier claimed that there was an attempt from the government to frame her issues as a matter of national security.

“Habang binabasa ko siya kanina, ako ay lubhang natawa. Nakakatawa dahil kabalintunaan ang kanyang mga sinasabi dito sa kanyang statement na may petsang October 20, 2026. Bakit nakakatawa? Pinag-uusapan dito ang patungkol sa may bandang dulo ay start working and stop politicking,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a media briefing.

(While I was reading it earlier, I was wholly laughing. It is funny because what she is saying here in her statement dated October 20, 2026 is ironic. Why is it laughable? She said here at the end to start working and stop politicking.)

“Kahit na nasa gitna tayo ng krisis ng Middle East, maraming kalamidad na humarap sa atin at sa ngayon ay may El Niño. Nandiyan ang Pangulo, hindi lang para managot ang dapat na managot, nagsusumikap, nagtatrabaho, pinapatupad ang batas para managot ang dapat na managot—isama na pati ang mga nagtatraydor sa bansa,” Castro said.

(Even if we are in the middle of the crisis in the Middle East, there are a lot of calamities in front of us and now where is the El Niño. The President is there, not just to hold the responsible to account, to try hard, to work, to implement the law to hold people into account—including those betraying the country.)
It was Duterte who has had several personal foreign trips, Castro said.

The Palace exec urged the public not to be distracted. While the Palace will not intervene with Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial at the Senate, she maintained that the prosecution has presented a lot of evidence. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Ombudsman suspends DICT exec over alleged conflict of interest in P1.55B contracts
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday placed Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Undersecretary for E-Government David Almirol Jr. under a six-month preventive…

blocks.text: The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday placed Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Undersecretary for E-Government David Almirol Jr. under a six-month preventive suspension over an alleged conflict of interest involving government contracts worth around P1.55 billion.

In its seven-page order, the Ombudsman said that the suspension stemmed from the pending administrative complaints of grave misconduct, conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service and a criminal complaint for alleged violation of Republic Act No. 6713 or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees.

The complaints were based on a report by the DICT Internal Audit Unit dated June 2025 flagging a possible conflict of interest involving the hiring of former Multisys personnel and the award of contracts to other related companies, considering that Almirol founded Multisys Technologies Corporation (Multisys) in 2010.

Almirol also served as its president and chief executive officer for more than a decade before his appointment as DICT Undersecretary for E-Government in August 2022 and would later lead the development and rollout of the eGovPH Super App.

“Further investigation of the Office of the Ombudsman revealed that at least eight DICT contracts were awarded to companies with financial relationships with Multisys. From November 2023 to May 2025, the DICT awarded eight eGov-related contracts to several related companies totaling to about P1.55 billion,” the Ombudsman said.

“These contracts covered information and communications technology consultancy, e-government application deployment, web-based messaging services, cloud infrastructure, data center colocation and software subscriptions,” the Ombudsman added.

In addition, the Ombudsman said Multisys’ audited financial statements showed revenues from the related companies for managed services, and that the audited financial statements report revenue from the other companies “for managed services of P110.8 million in 2023 and P514.6 million in 2024”.
Records also showed that Almirol did not divest immediately after his appointment to the DICT. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged vehicle attack as suspect appears in court
articles.summary: Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said on Wednesday, as the man accused of the attack appeared in…

image.caption: Helen Haines, an independent lawmaker in Australia, was struck twice by a car on Monday outside her electoral office, Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne on Monday. (Mick Tsikas/AAP/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said on Wednesday, as the man accused of the attack appeared in court.
Politician's husband says his wife is stable

Doctors amputated Haines's left leg after she was struck twice by a car in Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne, on Monday, Phil Haines said. They worked for days to save her right leg but were ultimately unsuccessful, he told a news conference in Melbourne.
"The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she's stable. That is the most important thing for our family," he said.

Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old resident of the rural town of Tarrawingee within Haines's electorate, was charged with three offences: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a public official.
Additional charges of cannabis cultivation and possession have also been laid against Nugent, court filings showed.
Phil Haines, left, Haines's husband, speaks to reporters alongside Australia's Governor General Sam Mostyn in Melbourne. (William West/AFP/Getty Images)
The suspect was restrained by members of the public at the scene before being arrested.
Haines, an independent lawmaker who has championed causes including climate change and regional housing, remains in critical condition.
Police are still investigating the motive for the rare attack on an elected official.
Appears in court

During a brief court appearance on Wednesday, the accused's lawyer said his client suffers from a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and was also being treated for concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. His lawyer told the magistrate his client had some mental health concerns and that it was his first time in custody.
There was no application for bail, and the case was deferred until Feb. 4.
Anti-terrorism police are among the agencies investigating the incident. While police allege the attack was "targeted," they say they believe it was an isolated incident.

There was no intelligence to suggest any threat to Haines, and the Australian Federal Police received no warning of any imminent danger from the alleged attacker, Commissioner Krissy Barrett told reporters.
"What I can say is we didn't have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon," she said.
Victoria state police said they could not find any direct past contact between Haines and the accused, with the motive still unknown.

"Motivation is one of these things that we absolutely need to explore. His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centerpiece of the investigation," Victoria Police Chief Mike Bush said.
Bush declined to comment on the man's mental health, saying the matter was before the court.

items: Man charged in vehicle attack on Australian MP

blocks.text: Haines had worked in nursing, midwifery and academia before being elected to Parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in both 2022 and 2025.

Violent attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, where federal lawmakers, state leaders and even prime ministers are often seen shopping, grabbing coffee or attending community events with relatively little security.

However, concerns about politicians' safety have grown in recent years amid rising political polarization, online abuse and threats against elected officials, prompting calls for greater protections while preserving the accessibility that has long characterized Australian politics.

articles.title: [DECODED] You no longer have to click anything to be targeted. But you can fight back.
articles.summary: With today's technological advances, malicious actors have found a way to get consumer data without you clicking on anything

blocks.text: With today's technological advances, malicious actors have found a way to get consumer data without you clicking on anything

items: The Cambridge Analytica scandal in 2018 revealed that the firm improperly accessed data from over 87 million Facebook users to target them for political campaigns, using tactics like viral quizzes to gather personal information.

Recent reports indicate that malicious actors, such as the Israeli firm Discover-Tech, have developed new methods to spy on users through online ads without requiring any user interaction, highlighting a shift in data privacy threats.

Maria Ressa's book, 'The Fight Back,' offers strategies for individuals and institutions to combat disinformation and protect democracy in the age of AI, emphasizing the importance of active engagement in data protection.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Remember when the Cambridge Analytica scandal blew up in 2018? It’s the data harvesting scandal that took place around 2014, where Cambridge Analytica had improperly accessed — and sold — the data of Facebook users to target them for political campaigns. Cambridge Analytica was a British political consultancy that worked for Donald Trump’s 2016 election campaign.

Facebook later reported that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data of over 87 million users, over 1.1 million of which were Filipinos. The data obtained included users’ phone numbers and contact lists, which allowed them to target not just the users who fell prey to the operations, but also their contacts who weren’t necessarily on their Facebook network.

How did they do it? Well, they had to be creative. They used those viral personality quizzes that tricked users into sharing details about themselves, perhaps convincing them that it was all in good fun. In reality, the firm used these details to profile, segment, and micro-target them for political campaigns.

Targeted advertising has been found to create isolation and division among consumers by limiting their exposure to diverse viewpoints and feedback — hence reinforcing what we now call “echo chambers.”
That happened over a decade ago. So much has changed in our information landscape since then, and malicious actors have gained other tools beyond social media platforms.
What if I told you that, with today’s technological advances, malicious actors have found a way to get consumer data without you clicking on anything?

Just last week, reports said that an Israeli digital advertising agency called Discover-Tech gave access to Candiru, a spyware company blacklisted by the US government, to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, and Russia’s Yandex. By doing so, Candiru was able to spy on internet users through a wide network of online ads, which only needed to load on the user’s side for the spying to occur. No clicks needed!

Two research groups, Citizen Lab and Confiant, separately investigated Discover-Tech and said that it utilized its data-sharing arrangements called cookie matching to track people. The researchers also said that some of its ads were used to help “plant spyware” on users’ devices.

Granted, the researchers said that the ads they found to be tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech’s overall volume. But the point stays the same: unlike the Cambridge Analytica scandal where users had to be coaxed into taking quizzes, there is now evidence that users don’t even have to do anything to be targeted by malicious actors. Simply being served an ad could be enough to compromise their personal details.

You might think that this is a problem for other countries, not for the Philippines. But recall that Cambridge Analytica had used the Philippines as a “petri dish” to test out its strategies before rolling it out to Western countries, thanks to our high social media usage and lack of regulation.

If you find this scary or at least alarming (like I do), Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa’s new book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators, is a good place to start.

In The Fight Back, Maria draws on her years on the frontlines against disinformation and Big Tech overreach and discusses in detail what citizens and institutions can do to understand, defend, and rebuild democracy in the age of AI.

She lays out 10 strategic goals across 10 chapters, each broken down into 10 concrete actions, to help people reclaim control over the technologies now shaping our lives — from mapping the battlefield and defending our communities to building a world where technology works for the people, not against us.
Maria discussed these and more in a conversation with WNYC’s Brian Lehrer for the second edition of Democracy Dialogues on October 16. You can watch Maria’s full interview here.

I hope this newsletter spooked you enough to take a more active role in protecting your own data and digital life. October, after all, is not only about Halloween. October is also cybersecurity awareness month. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard during Witkoff talks
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces years ago in Ukraine.

image.caption: Putin and Witkoff met in St. Petersburg for their ninth in-person talksImage: Kristina Solovyova/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of US captive Stephen Hubbard during talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.
Hubbard had been taken captive by Russian forces on charges of being a mercenary, which he denies. He was sentenced to seven years in prison at a closed trial in 2024.
Putin said Hubbard was at the airport and Witkoff said he was now "going home to his family."
US President Donald Trump later said that he had made the request directly to Putin during a phone call last week.

"The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia," Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform. "There was no 'swap' necessary for this release."

blocks.caption: A Russian court convicted Stephen Hubbard of being a mercenary in 2024, which he deniesImage: Moscow City Court press service/AFP

blocks.text: However, in a follow-up post, Trump also claimed that "numerous people" had called him to apologize after they criticized him for suspending a new round of sanctions, which he said was a necessary concession.
"If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt," Trump's post said.
Putin, Witkoff to discuss Ukraine peace deal
The release of Hubbard was seen as a goodwill gesture to the Trump administreation as the two sides discuss a peace deal in Ukraine.
"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff told Putin.
Putin proposed that Witkoff discuss the restoration of bilateral ties between Washington and Moscow, and the possibility of trilateral talks with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

The meeting — the ninth such talks between Witkoff and Putin —comes a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway, which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described as "positive."
"He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to ‌go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and ‌let's ​see if we can make some progress," he said ahead of the talks.
Witkoff to return to Oslo
Witkoff's meeting with Zelenskyy and other European leaders in Oslo has brought fresh momentum to peace efforts, more than 4 years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Ukrainian leader remained in Oslo on Wednesday where met with lawmakers in the Norwegian parliament.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said that Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for further consultations after his trip to St. Petersburg.
"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," he told Norway's public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.
Nevertheless, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow was willing to listen but that he didn't expect any "miracle." Trump on Tuesday reiterated that he wants Zelenskyy "to make a deal."

articles.title: UK approves Jackdaw gas field after years in limbo
articles.summary: Drilling is set to begin in the controversial North Sea plot as the government seeks to tackle high energy costs. Environmental groups have criticized the move and called for more clean energy.

image.caption: The Jackdaw gas field drilling venture had been approved by the Conservatives but held back by a Scottish courtImage: Adura/Handout/AFP

blocks.text: The UK government gave its approval for drilling to begin in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on Wednesday following years of legal and political problems that had blocked the controversial fossil fuel venture.
The Labour government justified the move saying it would strengthen the UK's energy security amid rising energy costs due to the US-Israeli war against Iran.
The gas field had previously been approved by the previous Conservative government, but wes held up by a Scottish court that said the approval had failed to consider carbon emissions.
The field lies about 150 miles (240 kilometres) east of Aberdeen in Scotland.
What did the UK government say about the Jackdaw approval?

Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump to increase drilling in the North Sea, said the new gas field would "protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter."
"At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help," he said.

"We're committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we'll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That's why we're taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea," Burnham added.

Energy Minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas could start flowing to British houses and businesses by the end of the month. It is expected that Jackdaw will increase domestic gas production by 6% and run for 11 years.
What has been the reaction to the UK's new gas project?
Shell, which is part of the Adura joint venture along with Norway's Equinor, welcomed the decision.
"Long-term energy projects depend on a competitive and stable investment environment, alongside timely and predictable regulatory decisions," Shell said.

However, the move has also been met with strong criticism. The Green Party called it "climate vandalism," while Greenpeace said the approval showed "the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy."

"True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates," said the environmental group's Ami McCarthy.
Critics have also questioned whether the new project would indeed have an impact on British gas bills since prices are determined by global energy markets.

blocks.caption: Protesters had called on Burnham to block approval for the Jackdaw gas fieldImage: Henry Nicholls/AFP

blocks.text: In an attempt to show the government's commitment to its climate targets, alongside the Jackdaw approval, it announced the set up of a new Energy Wealth Fund, with an initial £2 billion ($2.7 billion), aimed at channeling oil and gas revenues into funding the transition to cleaner energy.

The UK is targeting net zero emissions by 2050, although this target must be examined under the realities already facing the planet, with a new UN report saying the world is heading for 2.8 degrees of warming, way beyond the 1.5 degrees target set in the Paris Climate Agreement.
It also comes after the UK experienced its hottest ever summer on record, with temperatures hitting previously unheard of 38 degrees in some areas in June, according to the Met Office.

articles.title: Theater veteran Enchang Kaimo dies at 77
articles.summary: Kaimo co-founded the Christian theater company Trumpets in 1991

blocks.text: REST IN PEACE. Theater veteran Enchang Kaimo dies at 77.
Enchang Kaimo's Facebook page
Kaimo co-founded the Christian theater company Trumpets in 1991
MANILA, Philippines – Theater veteran Enchang Kaimo died on Monday, October 19, her husband, Mari Kaimo confirmed. She was 77.
“On this month 45 years ago, God brought me the helper who would be suitable for me. Today, He took her back unto Himself,” the actor and journalist wrote in a Facebook post.
“She rests now in His embrace and is fully free of the chains that bind us all. I look forward to the day that we are reunited once again when our Christ returns!” he added.

Enchang, whose full name is Maria Lorenza Dominguez Agudo-Kaimo, co-founded the Christian theater company Trumpets alongside Mari, Audie Gemora, Freddie Santos, and Luna Inocian in 1991. The group has produced plays and musicals like Joseph the Dreamer, The Lion, The Witch, and The Wardrobe, and The Little Mermaid, to name a few.

The theater great spent most of her theater career as an actress and a director. She helped bring to life the children’s musical Kings, Dreams & Schemes, and also performed in several musicals like Hairspray as the Female Authority Figure, The Wedding Singer as Rosie, and First Name Anew as Amy.

“Our dear Achi Enchang is now resting in perfect peace and rejoicing in the arms of her Lord & Savior. Chancel Rep has one less light, but heaven is rejoicing today,” Chancel Repertory Theatre wrote in its tribute to her.
Enchang is survived by her husband and their son, Khalil.
Her wake will be held on October 21 and 22 from 2 pm to 9 pm at the Lighthouse Christian Community, Buencamino Street, Barangay Cupang, Muntinlupa City. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Gambia to pay victims of Yahya Jammeh's rule from proceeds of his seized US mansion
articles.summary: The Gambia has confirmed receiving $2.5m from the sale of the house in Maryland.

blocks.text: On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property.
It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors".
Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results.
He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure.
Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office.
In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea.
A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts.
There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m.
Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.
A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents".

articles.title: US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors
articles.summary: As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace…

image.caption: In Iran rail transport has become important for moving goods as businesses contend with sanctions, regional tensions and disruptions to trade routesImage: Rouzbeh Fouladi/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult.
On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.
Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.
Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it.
Iran expands regional rail links

Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-officialMehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives.

The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year.
Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?
Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan, and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan.
The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies.
China-Iran rail traffic expands
Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days.

In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days.
For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz. But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences.

blocks.caption: Transiting the Strait of Hormuz has faced recurring and serious disruptions since the start of the US-Iran war earlier this yearImage: Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Delivery date cannot be guaranteed
A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability.
It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days.
The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran.
Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay.
Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries.
Rail works best for critical inputs
Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade.
"A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW.
Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport.
That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs whose absence can stop an entire production line.
US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran?
When delays become a cash problem
Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges.
For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit.
Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging.

If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived.
"Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it."
The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation.
Sanctions push trade toward other corridors
Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited.
Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels.
Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks.
"Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said.
That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices.
Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel.
Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight.

articles.title: Australian MP Helen Haines loses both legs after car attack as suspect appears in court
articles.summary: Doctors have amputated both of Helen Haines legs after the Australian lawmaker was hit in an apparent deliberate attack. The suspected driver involved in the attack has appeared in court.

image.caption: The attack on Helen Haines has shocked Australia and brought up questions of security for lawmakersImage: Martin Keep/AFP

blocks.text: Helen Haines, an Australian lawmaker struck by a car in an apparently deliberate attack on Monday, has lost both of her legs, her husband said on Wednesday.
Counterterrorism investigators have joined a police probe into the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne.

A 43-year-old suspect, Brendan N. from nearby Tarrawingee, appeared in Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.
Haines loses both legs after apparent attack

The independent MP underwent surgery on Monday night after suffering what were described as critical injuries in the incident, with national broadcaster ABC and the daily Sydney Morning Herald reporting on Tuesday that her left leg had been amputated.
Doctors then proceeded to amputate her right leg on Wednesday after having tried to save it.
"The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family," Phil Haines told reporters in Melbourne.
"We are grateful and thankful that at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape," he said.
What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines?
Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, which police said was a white Toyota, outside her office. She suffered serious injuries, particularly to her lower body.

ABC cited witnesses as saying they heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars. Later reports from witnesses said that after first pinning Haines against her own car, the driver reversed and rammed into her a second time.
The driver was arrested shortly after, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
Albanese said early investigations suggested the driver made a U-turn before hitting Haines as she was loading or unloading items at the trunk of her car.
"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," he told ABC.

The suspect's lawyer, Chirag Patel, told Magistrate Allison Vaughan on Wednesday that his client suffers from a rare neurological condition, as well as an undiagnosed mental health condition. He also said the defendant was suffering from a concussion.
Local barber ran to assist
Local barber Ricky Jeffries, whose shop is next to Haines' office, has been widely hailed as a hero after he ran to pull the driver out of the car and restrained him until police arrived.

blocks.caption: Barber Ricky Jefferies has been called a hero for restraining the driverImage: Seven Network/REUTERS

blocks.text: Jeffries downplayed his role, despite having intervened in what could have been a highly dangerous situation, as the man had a knife in the car.
"He [the driver] did have a knife. He didn't ​pull it ‌out. I just wasn't comfortable with his movements, and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away," he said.
Jefferies said he then held the man down until ‌police arrived.
"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and ‌he was ​no longer a threat, I just stood with him and I told him that he can't leave," he said.
Jefferies told journalists his first thought had been: "My wife would be disappointed if I'm injured."
"The other people here were just, they did so much more than me ... they deserve the credit," he added.
Political violence on the rise: PM Albanese
Albanese said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence.
"The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media."

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Albanese has said the incident seemed 'no accident'Image: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents."
At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery."

Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years.
Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action.
