articles.title: More than 1.5 million Canadian Crime Stoppers tips leaked, CBC exclusive finds

image.caption: Andrew Rivard is one of tens of thousands of Canadian tipsters whose personal information was exposed in the Crime Stoppers hack. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

blocks.text: When Andrew Rivard spotted a Crime Stoppers ad offering a $2,000 reward for tips in the winter of 2025, he decided to report what he knew about illegal cigarette sales in his neighbourhood.
Rivard’s original tip shows he disclosed his full name. He says he trusted the organization’s long-standing promise to protect the identities of all tipsters.
"I was told nothing would come of it; no one would come to me with, you know, I guess, resentment," Rivard said. "I just was hoping it would be that exactly — anonymous."

But the Manitoba man's report — along with information from more than 1.5 million other tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years — was exposed in a massive data breach, an exclusive CBC investigation has found.
The personal information captured in some compromised tips was detailed enough for CBC to contact more than a dozen tipsters — including Rivard — who reacted with shock and fear for their safety.
"It’s very scary, to be honest," said Rivard, who now worries his home address and phone number may be used by criminals for retaliation.
Rivard’s original tip as it appeared in the leaked data, including his full name. CBC retroactively redacted other personally identifiable information. (Valérie Ouellet/CBC)

The data was stolen last March by hacktivist collective Internet Yiff Machine. In a manifesto, the group said it wanted to disprove the claim by P3 Global Intel — the company hired by Crime Stoppers to manage its tips — that the platform was "anonymous" and "secure."

A copy of the hacked data was made available to researchers and journalists, including CBC, by Distributed Denial of Secrets, a U.S. non-profit that archives and publishes hacked and leaked documents it deems to be in the public interest.

CBC took extensive precautions to protect this sensitive data throughout its investigation. Our security measures included, but were not limited to, encryption and working in a self-contained, offline environment. The sensitive information was only accessible to a small number of CBC journalists working on the project. Ultimately, CBC intends to destroy its copy of the dataset.

Beyond confirming they were hacked over six months ago, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) and individual chapters have not spoken about the extent of the breach, only saying they await a detailed report from Navigate360, the company that owns the P3 platform.
This is the first time precise figures on how many Canadian tipsters were compromised in the breach — and the severity of the information exposed — have been made public.

items: Canadian investigation launched into data breach that exposed millions of IDs
Hacker took 100,000 documents in 2025 'cyber incident,' Kingston Police say

blocks.text: Our interviews and analysis of Canadian content in the leaked data suggest that Crime Stoppers, along with the company it contracted to manage its database, failed to protect tipsters' identities, left personal information unredacted and improperly retained decades of sensitive records.

"For a system that has been designed to promise anonymity to the users, that has failed categorically," said Prof. Ali Dehghantanha, the Canada Research Chair in Cybersecurity and Threat Intelligence at the University of Guelph.
He’s one of two experts who were shown our methodology and limited samples of the data from a secure CBC laptop.

After seeing CBC’s main findings, the RCMP shared concerns that the breach could “jeopardize public safety, including the safety of tipsters, individuals identified in tips and police officers," it said in a statement, adding it was originally told the leak did not include Canadian data or personal information.
CBC also shared the same information with the CCSA, which declined an interview.

In a written statement, the organization’s president, David J. Forster, said they “recognize the concern and uncertainty this incident has created, particularly for people who trust Crime Stoppers with sensitive information.”
There are currently 68 Crime Stoppers chapters registered as non-profits in Canada, according to data from the Canada Revenue Agency.
Professor Ali Dehghantanha is one of two cybersecurity experts who examined samples of the data. (Li Yanjun/CBC)
Tips about high-profile Canadian investigations

Crime Stoppers is a network of civilian-run non-profits that collects anonymous tips on crime and suspicious activity. It operates independently of law enforcement, though it refers a portion of tips back to them to assist in investigations.

The organization often appeals to the public, in partnership with police, for help with unsolved crimes and to advance investigations — all with the promise of anonymity for tipsters who contact them.

CBC’s analysis of Canadian tips found mentions of many high-profile cases that generated significant public attention — from Barry and Honey Sherman’s murders to Amber Tuccaro's disappearance, Montreal’s Luka Magnotta case and, more recently, the international manhunt for Ryan Wedding.

items: To see our methodology, scroll to the bottom of this story or click here.

blocks.text: Many of the tips dealt with serious allegations, with some people explicitly saying they feared retribution for speaking out.
Citizens called with information about alleged murderers, terrorists and pedophiles or incriminating details about people they were close to, like family members on the run or breaching court orders.

In 2012, police asked for the public’s help in identifying the voice of a man with a connection to missing Indigenous woman Amber Tuccaro. CBC found hundreds of tips mentioning her disappearance in the leaked Crime Stoppers tips. (Valérie Ouellet/CBC)

A third of all tips talked about drugs and drug trafficking; hundreds reported suspicious activity in their neighbourhoods, often naming individuals and implicating organized crime, biker gangs or drug cartels — including the Hells Angels, Rock Machine and Outlaws, as well as B.C.’s Red Scorpions and Independent Soldiers.

items: 'Surrey Six' murders mastermind Jamie Bacon released from prison

blocks.text: Notes in the data from Crime Stoppers staff suggest some of those tips led to real-life consequences: Nearly 49,000 tips were linked to a case cleared by an arrest or criminal charges, while nearly 1,000 tipsters were approved for cash rewards.
"I am concerned. I am really worried," said Dehghantanha, who has conducted digital forensics investigations for over a decade.
“I am really concerned about these records … being in the hands of the wrong people, while those people who have been impacted are not aware of that and do not have any support.”
Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database
That's exactly the situation one Canadian woman is facing. CBC agreed to withhold her identity given her safety concerns.
She gave a tip about the murder of a loved one, which was unsolved at the time.
"I just feel all the anxiety and scared feeling come back," said the woman. Police have now charged an individual with murder.
"They were capable of hurting my loved one. They could come back and hurt one of us."
Tipsters self-identified in over 4,300 tips, data suggests

More than 850,000 tips — about half of all Canadian records identified by CBC — included personally identifiable information about tipsters, individuals named in allegations and even Crime Stoppers staff and police.

Street addresses and phone numbers appeared most frequently, alongside tens of thousands of personal emails, licence plates and hundreds of banking details related to cash rewards — information that could all be used to uncover an individual's identity.
We could not determine in every instance whether the information belonged to a tipster, a victim or those accused of a crime.

However, CBC found that in over 4,300 reports, tipsters introduced themselves with a full name, although Crime Stoppers explicitly tells the public to avoid including identifying details. Still, this represented a fraction of reports, at less than one per cent of all entries over 25 years. CBC wasn't able to verify whether all names were legitimate.
In 2021, police sought the public's help in identifying a suspect caught on video near the home of billionaire philanthropists Barry and Honey Sherman. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
Despite hundreds of those tips containing clear staff warnings that a tipster had "self-identified" or had been "exposed," the information still appeared in the database unredacted.
Storing all these data points together is a gold mine for fraudsters, said Dehghantanha.
"Imagine I am calling you and talking about the tip that you have provided and asking for more information. Immediately, I build ... trust," he said.

items: Shock and surprise after FBI arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert in ShinyHunters hacking case

blocks.text: A name or phone number on a list might not seem like much, but it’s enough to do serious damage, said Ben Coon, chief intelligence officer of U.S. cybersecurity firm Unit 221B, who was also shown limited samples of the data.

"From what I saw, there's so much low-hanging fruit here that we could ask questions," said Coon, who said the data could be used for crimes ranging from financial fraud and extortion to money laundering.
Beyond what was collected, experts say the decision to store decades of historical tips in a single place defies basic data retention standards.
"If a tip is closed, does that need to stay online?" said Coon. "The answer to that, to me, is no."
Both experts agree that even though Crime Stoppers uses a third party to manage its data, it is still responsible for auditing how well it is secured.
"You can always outsource the operation … [and] the work," said Dehghantanha. "But you cannot outsource the accountability. You are always accountable when you are collecting the data."
Hacker claims data not publicly available online

Both cybersecurity experts said they were surprised CBC had found the data as they couldn’t locate copies of it online, which they said was reassuring. But they added that once a dataset has been leaked, it’s generally available somewhere.

In an email exchange with CBC News in September, someone purporting to represent Internet Yiff Machine wrote, "I briefly attempted to sell it publicly; however, changed my mind and no copy has made it into the public yet."
They added that the security measures of P3, which was storing Crime Stoppers' tips, were "terrible" and that the platform is still vulnerable.
"I wouldn’t trust [the hackers] at all," said Dehghantanha. "Selling [data] on the underground market is not that difficult, right…. There is a demand."
Internet Yiff Machine’s manifesto includes lines critical of police departments and for-profit prisons. (Valérie Ouellet/CBC)

In a statement, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association said, "If there is information within the leaked records that could identify people who submitted tips, it is an extremely serious issue." It added that protecting people's safety and anonymity is its "highest priority."

It did not directly comment on the precise figures shared by CBC, but said that it has been communicating with the third-party platform "to assess what records may have been affected, what personal information may have been exposed and what measures were taken to enhance the security of the platform."

"With regard to notifying individuals identified in the records, CCSA has concerns about doing so without jeopardizing the anonymity and safety of tipsters," it said, adding that "the information available to us does not distinguish people who submitted tips from people identified in them."
"We will share further verified information as it becomes available, while ensuring that our communications do not create additional risks for individuals."

Navigate360, the U.S.-based company that owns the P3 platform, did not respond to CBC's requests for comment, which included questions about what security measures it had taken since the hack, whether it had shared reports with Crime Stoppers about the compromised data and whether it was still collecting tips.

items: ShinyHunters hackers say they breached FBI, stole employee data
RCMP warn of new scam involving the purchase of gold

blocks.text: The RCMP told CBC that at the time of the leak, it was “advised that Canadian data had not been affected based on the results of the preliminary personally identifiable information (PII) assessment."
"Then, in May 2026, the RCMP was informed by Crime Stoppers that the data breach did include Canadian data but would not contain PII of persons who have reported.”
The national police service added that it is now “engaged with the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association to determine the full scope of the incident."

It stated that it has not received reports of anyone being threatened as a result of the breach and advised anyone with concerns about their submitted information to contact the organization or their local chapter.

The Toronto Police Service, which uses tips from Toronto Crime Stoppers — the chapter with the most tips in the leak — told CBC that the group had notified it of a hack in March, but that it "has not received any information indicating the safety of officers, tipsters or members of the public has been compromised."
As for Rivard, the Manitoba man whose tip was exposed in the leak, he says Crime Stoppers should have been more transparent.
"It might have been embarrassing, but own up to it, just tell the public, let them know, and they might have your trust after, they might not: Let them decide."
Methodology: How CBC identified Canadian tips in the Crime Stoppers hack

This investigation is based on CBC’s analysis of more than 8.3 million raw records leaked in March 2026. The breached data originated from P3 Global Intel, a U.S.-based tip management software owned by the company Navigate360. A copy of this hacked data was released to journalists, including CBC, by Distributed Denial of Secrets, a non-profit whistleblower site that publishes hacked documents it deems to be in the public interest. The data contains unverified criminal allegations that have not necessarily been investigated by police or proven in court.
CBC considered a tip to be Canadian if it was submitted to a Canadian Crime Stoppers chapter or contained specific Canadian geographic and linguistic references.

We identified a grand total of 1.6 million records using these combined methodologies. The vast majority were tips submitted directly to Canadian Crime Stoppers chapters (97.98%). The remaining 32,000 tips (2.02%) were submitted to U.S. and international Crime Stoppers chapters, but they all contained Canadian references, such as city names, postal codes, phone area codes or the names of government institutions.
The data was compared against a list compiled by our team of over 700 crime-related keywords, including the names of victims, suspects, missing persons and high-profile police operations.

For this analysis, CBC defined personal identifying information (PII) as: a tipster’s full name, any complete street address, postal code, direct phone number, personal email, vehicle licence plate, personal social media account and/or banking details. Publicly advertised phone numbers of Crime Stoppers chapters and police departments, as well as general switchboards, tiplines, hotlines, general emails and the physical addresses of chapters and police departments were excluded from our PII analysis.

We used Google’s Gemini AI to help us draft, troubleshoot and optimize computer programming scripts in Python and SQLite to structure and systemically analyze a dataset too massive to process manually, (e.g. with spreadsheets). Every suggestion, piece of logic, and code generated by Gemini was independently reviewed by our data journalist to ensure integrity and adherence to CBC’s Journalistic Standards and Practices. All data outputs were rigorously audited in the same way. The interface was strictly used to generate computer code and was not permitted to make autonomous decisions, run the code itself or access the source database at any time.

CBC/Radio-Canada's corporate agreement with Gemini stipulates that our data is kept strictly private. None of our prompts, uploaded files or chats can be used to improve Google's AI models, and no human reviewers can access our conversations.
Methodology, coding and data analysis by Valérie OuelletData analysis and additional research by Michelle Allan

articles.title: Canadian housing market 'on its knees' as odds of Bank of Canada rate hike rise
articles.summary: The Bank of Canada has not raised interest rates since July 2023. And while an eighth-consecutive hold is widely-predicted next week, a growing number of economists and traders are now expecting the…

image.caption: Experts say a rate hike from the Bank of Canada on Oct. 28 would have significant impacts on the country's battered real estate market. (Michel Aspirot/CBC/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Business·New

The Bank of Canada has not raised interest rates since July 2023. And while an eighth-consecutive hold is widely-predicted next week, a growing number of economists and traders are now expecting the central bank to hike its trend-setting rate to tamp down stubborn inflation.
A rate hike in October would have significant impacts on Canada's battered real estate market, experts say
The Bank of Canada has not raised interest rates since July 2023.

And while an eighth-consecutive hold is widely-predicted next week, a growing number of economists and traders are now expecting the central bank to hike its trend-setting rate to tamp down stubborn inflation.

Mortgage and debt experts say higher rates would have significant impacts on Canada's sagging real estate market. Payments on variable-rate mortgages would rise immediately, along with rates for new fixed mortgages. The pool of eligible buyers would shrink, shifting power from sellers to those who can qualify for the financing needed to make a purchase. Home prices could dip lower.

"The housing market is kind of on its knees right now, and rising rates is like tossing a drowning guy an anchor," said Scott Terrio, manager of consumer insolvency at Ontario-based Hoyes Michalos & Associates.
He says a hike "would reverberate massively."
Could an interest rate hike see home prices fall?
The volume of home sales nationwide is currently at a 25-year low, says Ben Rabidoux of Ontario-based Edge Realty Analytics.
He describes confidence among buyers today as "unbelievably weak across the country," owing to a slew of economic uncertainties ranging from the Canada-U.S. trade war to the impact of AI on jobs.
"The reality is that when we look at per capita home sales, we're already back to 1990s levels, which [was] a really terrible recessionary environment."
On home prices, Rabidoux believes "a gradual grind lower over the next three or six months is very plausible" if interest rates start rising.
That perfect Ontario real estate listing might be staged by AI. Here's what to watch for
Last week, the Canadian Real Estate Association downgraded its forecast for 2026 home sales activity for a third straight quarter.
The industry group referenced a "notably more hawkish tone from the Bank of Canada," as it called for 444,530 homes to be sold by year-end, a 5.2 per cent drop from 2025.
The Bank of Canada's policy rate has stood still at 2.25 per cent since a quarter-point cut in October 2025.

Governor Tiff Macklem has recently warned the bank may need to raise borrowing costs if energy prices remain elevated. On Saturday, he said there is "no resolution in sight for the conflict in the Middle East" that has roiled global energy markets for the past several months.

items: CREA revises down 2026 home sales forecast again as September transactions fall 7.7% over same month last year
Inflation rises to 3.1% in September, as fuel prices push higher: StatsCan

blocks.text: On Monday, the latest inflation data from Statistics Canada put a spotlight on soaring energy costs. The report showed rising fuel prices have yet to meaningfully spill into other sectors of the economy. However, the Bank of Canada's latest survey, also released on Monday, found businesses are bracing for higher prices.
Odds of rate hike 'not a slam dunk'

The consensus in a recent Bloomberg survey still points to a hold, but so far this week, the Bank of Montreal, RBC Dominion Securities and Desjardins Group have flipped their predictions for Oct. 28 from a hold to a hike.

According to Bloomberg data, traders in the overnight swap market now put the odds of a 25-basis point rate hike from the Bank of Canada next week at 87 per cent, up from 70 per cent earlier this week. Swap market data measures the gap between today's interest rate and the future rate traders are betting on.
Canada's economy still resilient, but U.S. trade war taking its toll
Derek Holt, head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, is among those calling for a rate hike.
"It's not a slam dunk call, but there is probably enough supporting evidence for a hike," he wrote in a research note on Monday.
Macquarie Group economist David Doyle agrees. He predicts the Bank of Canada will raise its policy rate by 125 basis points by the end of 2027.
"Our baseline case remains for a rate hike at this month's meeting," he wrote in a note to clients on Monday. "We continue to see a steady rate hike cycle ahead."

items: Deloitte Canada cuts GDP growth forecast by 20% as tariffs grip economy amid Trump's trade war
No Canada-U.S. trade deal expected before American midterm elections: sources

blocks.text: Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and an expert commentator with LowestRates.ca, agrees.
"If there is a hike, I do think it's gonna be a cycle," Zlatkin said.
She points to a recent price drop in the notoriously expensive Greater Toronto Area as a sign that now is a "good time to buy."
"There's a possibility [that] housing prices are going to continue falling, but the reality is, if you'll qualify for the property today, then you'll qualify again later on if rates rise."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse set up Marketplace sale without telling him — and gave out his address
articles.summary: A Toronto man is warning Canadians to think twice before sharing too much personal information with Muse, Meta’s AI agent that acts as a personal assistant, after he says it arranged a Marketplace…

blocks.text: Montreal

A Toronto man is warning Canadians to think twice before sharing too much personal information with Muse, Meta’s AI agent that acts as a personal assistant, after he says it arranged a Marketplace sale without his knowledge and provided a stranger with his home address.
Cybersecurity experts warn of potential data risks, urge caution
He used Meta’s AI agent Muse for Marketplace sales. Then it set one up behind his back
Matt Robb started using Meta’s new AI agent Muse to handle his Facebook Marketplace transactions.
But after listing a keyboard for sale, he got a bit more than he bargained for.
“I was like, ‘Oh God, OK... This isn’t good,” he said of the moment he realized Muse had set up a sale and given his home address to a stranger on Marketplace without his knowledge.

“Muse doesn’t check with me, it doesn’t tell me this guy has messaged and then it gives the guy my address, agrees to his price and literally tells him to come right now, that’s the crazy part,” Robb said.
When the buyer showed up, Muse even told him, “Yep I’m here!” on Robb’s behalf, when he wasn’t home.
A screenshot of the interaction between Robb's Muse agent and the buyer on Facebook Marketplace. (Submitted by Matt Robb)
'Your data is not secure’: cybersecurity expert
Muse is an artificial intelligence agent run by Meta — Facebook and Instagram’s parent company.

It acts as a virtual personal assistant, promising to stay on top of your emails, buy your kids’ school supplies and even rebook an upcoming flight, all in exchange for access to your most sensitive data.
But behind the cuddly face, experts say, there is danger.
“All these big companies, they're in it for your data,” said Éric Parent, a cybersecurity expert. “The answer is no, your data is not secure.”
Meta’s Muse is an AI agent which acts as a virtual personal assistant. (Meta)
Parent says not only is your data at risk, but also the data of those who communicate with you.
“A person who wrote you an e-mail or sent you a text message is expecting that message to go to your eyes,” Parent said.

“Now, overnight, you can be emailing somebody and they've actually granted access to a major corporation to actually sift through your emails. That's going to be an uncomfortable thing down the road.”
Parent advises you to really look at what you’re giving Muse access to and ask yourself what the impact can be if it takes an action on your behalf.
“You have to put it to the worst case scenario,” Parent said.
Pay attention to permissions
Meta says the data and credentials Muse collects is securely stored, adding Muse will always check with you first for sensitive actions like purchases or sending an email.
When asked how a situation like Robb’s could have happened, a spokesperson for Meta pointed CBC to a social media post by Robb, who shared his ordeal on X.

Robb explained he had clicked on "Allow always" instead of "Allow one time" when asking Muse to handle his Marketplace transactions, and by doing so, he says it granted the AI permission to send messages on his behalf going forward, using a template it put together with information it asked from him.
“Which also included the pick-up address that I did give to Muse,” Robb wrote in his post, adding he didn’t think it would send his address out “to everyone that gave me an offer.”
“I mentioned to the Meta team it could be easily overlooked as it was with me and they said they will be making this more clear moving forward.”

items: What could possibly go wrong with Meta's Muse?

blocks.text: In a tweet replying to Robb’s post, David Singleton, the co-founder and CEO of Meta Superintelligence Labs wrote: “Glad that we were able to confirm together that there was no breach of privacy controls.”
In an email to CBC, Meta said Muse runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else’s agent can reach it.
“That is where Muse lives and where the data and credentials for any service a person connects are securely stored,” a Meta spokesperson wrote.
But Meta has a history of mishandling its users’ personal information, even facing fines totalling hundreds of millions of euros in Europe.

items: Time for a digital divorce? Trade war puts spotlight on Canada's relationship with U.S. big tech

blocks.text: Another concern is that Meta is subject to the U.S. CLOUD Act, which gives the American government the authority to access data maintained in a server owned by a U.S. company.
Lawyer Jean-François Latreille says it’s a privacy concern.
“That would mean that technically, the American government could have access to privacy information that is being stored on these systems,” he said.
Quebecers protected by strict data privacy legislation
But Latreille says Quebecers are protected by Law 25, Canada’s strictest data privacy legislation.
Under Law 25, if a company fails to keep personal information safe, it can be fined up to $25 million or the amount corresponding to four per cent of its global revenue.
Latreille says Quebecers who believe their rights are violated can file a complaint any time directly with Meta’s privacy officer or by addressing the Quebec Access to Information Commission.
The commission told CBC in an email it urges individuals to always exercise caution when sharing their personal information.

“Today’s practices and mechanisms for collecting and exchanging information mean that large amounts of personal information are held and circulate widely, posing growing risks to individuals’ privacy,” wrote a spokesperson.
A screenshot of Robb and Muse's interaction after Robb found out about the Marketplace transaction. (Submitted by Matt Robb)
As for Robb and his keyboard, he told the buyer what happened and they rescheduled another meeting — one he was privy to.
Robb also says Muse admitted to giving out his address without his explicit authorization.
Now, he's warning others not to share too much personal information to avoid a stranger showing up at their door unannounced.
“It could happen to someone more vulnerable, right?” he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Gloria has been a journalist in Montreal for more than a decade. Prior to joining CBC, she reported in three languages and five different countries for Global News, France 24, Berliner Zeitung and Diario La Tribuna in her native Honduras.

articles.title: Problem gambling jumps, suicides triple in Ontario after expansion of online casinos
articles.summary: Nearly 130,000 Ontarians now show signs of problem gambling, compared to some 43,000 in 2018, a tripling of the number of people who meet the criteria of gambling too frequently, losing money and…
articles.byline: Dave Seglins, Andreas Wesley, Saloni Bhugra

image.caption: The number of problem gamblers in Ontario has spiked and gambling-related suicides have tripled since the expansion of private online casino games and sports betting in 2022, CBC News has learned. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Investigates

Nearly 130,000 Ontarians now show signs of problem gambling, compared to some 43,000 in 2018, a tripling of the number of people who meet the criteria of gambling too frequently, losing money and struggling with addiction, CBC News has learned.
CBC News investigates public health impact of online games, sports betting
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 21, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.
Anna, a 51-year-old single mother of two teens, says online slot machine games cost her nearly everything.
And even at that point, the Ontario resident says it was hard to stop.
"The amount of money that I spent and lost — it was astronomical," she told a recent meeting of Gamblers Anonymous in Toronto, which CBC News was invited to witness.
The peer support group has been a lifeline that helped her stop betting and break free from inducements and marketing she would receive from the betting apps, she says.
"If I had gone a little while without gambling, they would literally send me thousands of dollars to say 'free money' to keep you going," she recalled.
Gamblers Anonymous helped 'Anna' kick her addiction
She’s not alone.
The number of problem gamblers in Ontario has spiked and gambling-related suicides have tripled since the expansion of private online casino games and sports betting in 2022, CBC News has learned.

Nearly 130,000 Ontarians now show signs of gambling problems, compared with roughly 43,000 in 2018, a tripling of the number of people who meet the criteria of gambling too frequently, losing money and struggling with addiction.

These estimates are based on new research from the Alberta Gambling Research Institute (AGRI), which found a 0.5 per cent jump in Ontario’s rates of problem gambling compared to 2018. Their analysis uses the "Problem Gambling Severity Index" and data from Statistics Canada’s 2025 Canadian Community Health Survey.

AGRI researcher Carrie Shaw says the research is "brand new" and significant, showing that six months after Ontario’s private casinos opened in 2022, the number of problem gamblers in the province climbed while dropping in the rest of Canada.
"In Ontario’s market, gambling is very much normalized through access and advertisements," said Shaw, who presented her findings at an AGRI conference in May.
"It's true across Canada, but more so in Ontario, given the amount of exposure there is," she said.
Carrie Shaw of the Alberta Gambling Research Institute found rising rates of problem gambling in Ontario after the 2022 online expansion of online betting. (CBC)
In July, Alberta joined Ontario in legalizing online gambling run by private companies. Everywhere else in Canada, it is illegal.

"With online gambling ... the barriers to access are completely removed. You can access it anytime from your computer, your mobile phone, any time of day or night," Shaw said. "You can be sitting at your desk at work and still be engaging."
Gambling suicides rising
The Office of the Chief Coroner of Ontario also reports a spike in gambling-related suicides in the years after Ontario began allowing online betting.
Before Ontario’s expansion, the province had an average of five gambling-related suicides each year from 2016 to 2021. That number tripled after 2022.

Matthew Young, chief research officer for non-profit gambling research network Greo Evidence Insights, says he called on government two years ago to do a better job of tracking online gambling activity for fear of increased addiction, bankruptcies and suicides.
"We warned that we might be seeing the harms that we're now seeing in the data," he said.
Those calls were ignored, he says.

A study published in the September 2026 American Journal of Preventive Medicine found a dramatic jump in the number of people with gambling disorders showing up at Ontario hospital emergency departments in distress.

A March 2026 study in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ) found a 95.5 per cent increase in men and boys making gambling-related calls to ConnexOntario, the province's 24-hour mental health and addictions help line, over the last decade.

items: More people are seeking emergency care for gambling, a new study says — and it's mostly men and boys
Sharp rise in young men contacting Ontario gambling helpline, researchers find

blocks.text: Young calls it "unfathomable" that Canada changed the Criminal Code to allow online gambling and that provinces are opening their markets without proper study of the potential public health impacts.
Gambling researcher says Canada needs better addiction monitoring

Young says that amid lobbying to legalize online gambling in other provinces, he would like to see better monitoring and for a share of the billions in revenues to be dedicated to independent research into ways to curb addiction and gambling-related harms.
Greo Evidence Insights was formerly known as the Ontario Problem Gambling Research Centre.
Ontario defunded it in 2019.
Are you, or someone you know, suffering from gambling? Support is available.

items: ConnexOntario 1-866-531-2600 or Text CONNEX to 247247
Gamblers Anonymous 1-855-222-5542 or visit Canada or Toronto/GTA

articles.title: How this figure skating season will 'set the stage' for Canada's next Olympic generation
articles.summary: Canada has won just one Olympic figure-skating medal since 2018, a 2026 bronze from ice-dance duo Piper Gilles and Paul Poirier, who are taking the year away from competition. In charge of…

image.caption: Olympic champion Gabrielle Daleman can be a guide which bridges Canada’s most recent golden generation to what could possibly be its next. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada has won just one Olympic figure-skating medal since 2018, a 2026 bronze from ice-dance duo Piper Gilles and Paul Poirier, who are taking the year away from competition. In charge of shepherding that next wave of talent to the Olympic podium is CEO Therese Brisson, who took over the role in July after spending six years in the same position at Alpine Canada.
'I do think we should be ambitious,' says Skate Canada CEO Therese Brisson
It’s Day 1 of the school year.

Freshmen are just stepping onto campus, wide-eyed about the next four years. Some seniors have returned for a victory lap. Juniors are back in a familiar place, now experienced and knowledgeable on how to proceed.
Smush it all together, and the atmosphere feels light. Opportunities abound. Some will succeed and others will fail, but that will all be determined in due time.

That’s where we find Canadian figure skating as a new season — and a new Olympic quadrennial — begins with the Grand Prix de France on Friday. The Skate Canada International follows the week after. Live coverage of both events will be available CBCSports.ca and CBC Gem, starting Friday at noon ET / 9 a.m. PT.

“Going into this season, it's really just taking it in and enjoying the time and enjoying the training and the ups and downs and just being back on the circuit and getting to do a home nationals this year,” said Gabrielle Daleman, a figurative senior on the team who returned in 2025 after two seasons away.

“It's just really taking in those moments because I am close to the end. I don't know how much longer my body wants to keep doing this. I would always do it for the rest of my life if I could. So just really being grateful for every moment.”

items: Canadian figure skater Gogolev still discovering full potential after breakout season

blocks.text: Daleman, the 28-year-old Torontonian, said her confidence, something she views as a conscious being — “she likes to come and go” — is high.
Especially since the weight of an Olympic year is now gone.

“I can't lie. I really did not enjoy it last season. I went into it and I was like, ‘Oh, I'm just going to take it every moment.’ No, we were stressy. We were depressy. We were lemon zesty. That's my favourite saying. I think I cried for like three weeks straight in December. I was like, mom, dad, you need to come down and see me. Like, I'm not functioning.”

“And it was honestly very overwhelming because I went from being so incredibly injured for three years to like, hey, you've got nine months to re-walk, relearn to skate, get your jumps back in shape and try to qualify. And I was like, this was my idea? This is not one of my greatest.”
Gabrielle Daleman shares her favourite figure skating element

Daleman, who did not qualify for 2026 Milano-Cortina Olympics, is the last member of Canada’s national team who competed at the indelible 2018 Winter Games, when Tessa Virtue and Scott Moir’s ice-dance gold headlined a four-medal haul.

items: Grand Prix France opens new Olympic cycle with reshaped figure skating field

blocks.text: She was just 20 then, a veritable freshman and part of the team-event squad that won gold. Now, she’s a vet.

“I don't know if it's a role. I'm more just kinda through the looking glass. I'm loving seeing the new generation come up. I'm still trying to get to know everyone and make sure I meet them in one way or another, but I'm really just being like, ‘Wow, like we have really good talent coming up,’” Daleman said.
Canada's Gabrielle Daleman 'excited' to return to Grand Prix circuit for 1st time since 2022
Next wave of talent
In charge of shepherding that next wave of talent to the Olympic podium is CEO Therese Brisson, who took over the role in July after spending six years in the same position at Alpine Canada.
Brisson, the 60-year-old from Montreal, also competed at a pair of Olympics herself, capturing silver in 1998 and gold in 2002 as a member of Canada’s national women’s hockey team.
Canada has won just one Olympic figure-skating medal since 2018, a 2026 bronze from ice-dance duo Piper Gilles and Paul Poirier, who are taking the year away from competition.
Since 2022, only one active Canadian individual or team has climbed the podium at worlds, with pairs partners Lia Pereira and Trennt Michaud taking bronze earlier this year.

“As we look ahead, and part of the task here is to renew the strategic plan, I do think we should be ambitious. I look at the athletes and the athlete pool. We have more rinks per capita than any other nation, we have the best coaches in the world — the world comes here to be with our coaches. And if we have athletes with the same ambition, determination and work ethic, there's no reason why we shouldn't be competing with the world's best and really a world-leading nation in skating,” Brisson said.

items: Canadian pair Lia Pereira, Trennt Michaud skate to world bronze medal
Pereira and Michaud secure 8th-place pairs finish in Olympic debut

blocks.text: Brisson said the goal for Skate Canada should be to contend for three to four medals each Olympics, with an underlying system that replenishes itself and prevents lulls.

Among the biggest early changes was the announcement that high-performance director Mike Slipchuk would be transitioning out of the position after this season after 20 years at the helm. A replacement has not yet been named.
“The goal this year is to set the stage for 2030, and just as importantly 2034, because rebuilding that pool of athletes with podium potential takes time,” Brisson said.

Therese Brisson, right, said the goal for Skate Canada should be to contend for three to four medals each Olympics, with an underlying system that replenishes itself and prevents lulls. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
Canada has young team
With a young team across the board, there is plenty of potential for skaters to prove this season that they could be podium threats in the French Alps in 2030.

Young pairs duos Jazmine Desrochers and Kieran Thrasher or Ava Kemp and Yohnatan Elizarov could take a step forward in their rookie seasons on the Grand Prix circuit. Newly formed ice-dance team Marjorie Lajoie and Jean-Luc Baker, who previously competed for the U.S., may display quick chemistry.

items: More figure skating coverage

blocks.text: In singles, the likes of Fée Ann Landry and Sara-Maude Dupuis will be on the senior Grand Prix circuit, while juniors like Lia Cho have already shown great promise.
Jazmine Desrochers, top, and partner Kieran Thrasher, bottom, could take a step forward in their rookie season on the Grand Prix circuit. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
Meanwhile, Pereira and Michaud, women’s skater Madeline Schizas, men’s skater Stephen Gogolev and others will look to continue building through the primes of their careers.

This season, though, is about learning. Daleman will find out what she has left. Brisson will get to know the talent she’ll be working with. And the next generation of skaters will continue to discover whether they possess what it takes to reach Olympic medal-contender status.
To that end, Olympic champion Daleman can be a guide, bridging Canada’s most recent golden generation to what could possibly be its next.

“I just try to help, and when someone's going through a tough time, letting them know it can get better and do not give up,” Daleman said. “And if you keep your head down and put in the work, it will show.”

blocks.text: Republicans push back on Donald Trump’s wavering support for Ukraine
Ariana Baio

Overnight, a handful of Republicans have spoken out against Donald Trump’s softening stance on Russia, threatening to pull financial support for his agenda over his “embarrassing” handling of the Ukraine war.

blocks.caption: President Donald Trump is reflected in protective glass after speaking at a campaign rally at Pitt–Greenville Airport. Photograph: Matt Ramey/AP

blocks.text: Don Bacon, an outgoing congressman in Nebraska, condemned Trump’s actions – which include a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel and the pausing of sanctions on Moscow – as “absolutely disgraceful” and accused the US president of cozying up to a “war criminal” in Vladimir Putin, his Russian counterpart.
“It really is disgraceful, and the Republicans that I associate with, there’s a lot of us, can’t stand it,” Bacon told CNN on Monday. “I think the president’s leverage in this Congress is shot.”

Last week, Trump waived sanctions imposed on Russia through a law named after his longtime ally and late senator Lindsey Graham. The legislation, which he signed only last month, was intended to increase financial pressure on Russia, more than four years after it invaded Ukraine.

Instead, Trump announced he had struck a deal with Putin to import diesel fuel, which has become more expensive for Americans largely due to Trump’s war with Iran. Trump has previously blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russia.

articles.title: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
articles.summary: Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.
Phil Haines said the"horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".
The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.

Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.
Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.
"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."

He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.
"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.

Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.
Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.
He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.
In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.
The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.
Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
"His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush.
"Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."
Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.
Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.

Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable".
The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him.
Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured.
"Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun.
"She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme.
Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs.
Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters.
The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare.
Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident.
In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape.
There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said.
Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs.
Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing.
Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said.
Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better".
"We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says.
"Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency."

articles.title: Soft-spoken David Pocock has big ambitions – but first he wants politicians to ‘double down’ on kindness
articles.summary:
Independent senator’s goals ‘much bigger’ than prime ministership, he reveals in first speech to national press club

  • Get our

blocks.text: He’s six foot tall and full of muscle, but David Pocock’s real strength is often sounding like the most sensible, commonsense voice in the room.

At his first speech to the national press club on Wednesday, he said he wasn’t launching a bid for prime minister – no matter how much some people might like the softly spoken senator to have more say in federal politics.

Indeed, Pocock said he was already thinking about life after politics, admitting “you can’t do this for ever”. But before the full-time whistle on his parliamentary career, the former rugby star has a match against his toughest opponent yet: the two-party system.
“I want to be part of building a political system that actually delivers for Australians, no matter who is prime minister,” the ACT senator said.
“I see an opportunity at the next election for a new kind of community political collective … I want to use what I’ve learned over the past four-and-a-half years to help.”

He called for a higher calibre of politics after the alleged attack on the independent Indi MP Helen Haines. He branded parliament’s question time a “disgrace”, urging a “better standard” among colleagues “to take some of the edge off it”.

blocks.caption: Helen Haines the 'MP we all wish we had' says David Pocock – video

blocks.text: Speaking directly about Haines, he said parliament must “meet this [alleged] attack on you by doubling down on the values you represent” – listing transparency, accountability and kindness.

In front of staff and allies – the ACT politician Thomas Emerson, Pocock’s former staffer and lookalike, as well as the Cheek Media founder and Grayndler independent candidate, Hannah Ferguson – he called for three key policy reforms:

items: A 25% tax on gas exports, which he said could fund anything from boosting welfare to health reforms and aged care.
A 5% levy on datacentres to capture more benefits from the AI boom.
Transparency reforms to shine a light on lobbyists, secret meetings with politicians and vested interests.

blocks.text: Just two months of gas tax revenue would pay for 100,000 home support packages, while prosthetic eyes and noses for cancer victims would be paid for in three hours, he said. Pocock recounted the moment a woman sat sobbing in his office, so destitute on the miserable jobseeker allowance that she ate dog food because she hadn’t eaten meat in so long.
“A 25% gas export tax could help change that, allowing us to have a social security system that keeps people above the poverty line,” he said.

All politicians have these stories, even if not all of them talk about them with such emotion. Politics is a series of choices and priorities and, presented by Pocock in this way, the choice not to fund welfare boosts or aged care or cancer care is hard to justify.
Asked later about calls for budget discipline and cutting spending, Pocock replied instantly: “You can make cuts, or you can grow revenue.”
“I don’t understand why we’re slugging everyday Aussies and yet we’re happy to export gas for free.”

Despite having only one vote in parliament, and no longer holding Senate balance of power, Pocock has been extraordinarily successful in drawing attention to his key issues. Labor members are not his biggest fans, but he has moulded the gas tax narrative to the point that government MPs’ social media feeds are flooded with comments demanding change.
after newsletter promotion

Bending the national conversation around a complicated resources tax, to the point where the actual prime minister has to wade through swathes of comments from political normies on every post, shows some level of leadership. Not that Pocock is angling to win that position himself; for one, he said he’s staying in the Senate, not switching to the lower house.
For another, when he told the audience “don’t get ahead of yourselves with ‘Pocock launches bid for PM’ headlines”, it got only the second-biggest laugh in the room.
The biggest laugh came when he added: “My ambition is much bigger than that.”

His idea for a new “coalition” of independents was light on detail, but he said he wanted to “build” something alongside communities which were already organising. Pocock suggested an alliance of independents and collectives like the Community Strong movement headlined by Zali Steggall and Allegra Spender, going on to shout out independent tilts in ACT electorates of Bean, Canberra and Fenner, where his local campaign infrastructure could make a difference, but also the seat of Fisher and even Anthony Albanese’s, Grayndler.
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has said he wants his party to replace Labor. A Pocock-backed independent in Ferguson, replacing the prime minister in his own seat, would be a whole new level.
“I believe a model of smaller, community interest parties and independents working together in an alliance can succeed here and build the kind of future we want,” Pocock said.

Where that ends up, and if it gets off the ground, will be seen in coming months and years. Just don’t expect to see Pocock – rugby star, conservationist, senator, father – add prime minister to his CV anytime soon.

articles.title: Football: German coach Hürzeler flying high in Premier League
articles.summary: Fabian Hürzeler is younger than his star player, a fellow Premier League German. But, contrary to his reputation in his homeland, Hürzeler has become a popular figure both on and off the pitch in…

image.caption: Fabian Hürzeler masterminded a 3-0 win over champions Arsenal earlier this seasonImage: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/IMAGO

blocks.text: "We are absolutely in love with him. He's been an incredible manager. The results are extraordinary and we're flying."
Those words from Ben Parker will be familiar to fans of any club who have been on the kind of winning run Brighton and Hove Albion are currently on.
But all the signs on and off the pitch suggest that the man in question — Brighton's German coach Fabian Hürzeler — is more than just a flash in the Premier League pan.

Hürzeler has never coached in the Bundesliga. After winning promotion to Germany's top flight with St. Pauli in 2024, he left to become the youngest man ever to take charge in England's Premier League at 31. His team currently sit third, having won six games in a row including a 5-0 thrashing of bitter rivals Crystal Palace last weekend.

It was the repeat of a fixture last season that marked Hürzeler's lowest Brighton ebb, with a 1-0 home loss making it one win in 12. "There are only two options," the German coach said at the time. "Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life."
Fan relationship a two way street for Hürzeler

Parker, the co-editor of Brighton and Hove Albion fanzine, Dogma, admitted to DW that there were plenty who were not sure that persisting was the answer. "There was some disquiet at the end of that game, there were people shouting: 'You're getting sacked in the morning.'"
While such sentiment may be difficult to swallow for many coaches, Parker said that Hürzeler told him in an interview soon after joining the club that he welcomed it when needed.

"He talked about wanting a fan relationship that had a two way aspect. The club and him are really ambitious, so if the performances aren't up to scratch we should be telling him that. And that's what happened on that day. I see the whole thing as being quite healthy."

Hürzeler never played at the top level. He represented Germany's youth teams and turned out for Bayern Munich's reserves but soon grew frustrated with second-team football. He then accepted a player-coach role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23, which he performed alongside a job at an art dealership in Bavaria, where he moved with his family at the age of two having been born in the US.
Age and playing career no barrier to progress

That unusual path to top-flight management and some innovative tactics at St. Pauli led to a perception in Germany that Hürzeler was a little aloof and something of a 'laptop manager' in the vein of former Bayern Munich and Germany boss, Julian Nagelsmann who had a similarly nondescript playing career. This, so the charge goes, meant he wasn't able to forge the relationships and togetherness needed to make a team more than the sum of its parts.

That was rarely what was reported by his players and staff at St. Pauli, nor is it Hürzeler's belief. "I want to be myself, I don't want to play a role, and my age definitely helps regarding understanding the players," he said.

blocks.caption: Hürzeler was a popular figure at St. Pauli, who he led back to the Bundesliga Image: Axel Heimken/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I always say I speak their language and I understand their thoughts, because it wasn't that long ago when I played."

His antics on the sideline also earned him a reputation as a bit of a hot-head. Hürzeler was booked seven times during St. Pauli's promotion push and since joining Brighton, the German has been booked nine times and been sent off once. When asked about this, he said: "Emotions are part of the game."
Parker said this authenticity has also been reflected in his relationship with Brighton and Hove, on the south coast of England.
German duo take center stage

"For most Brighton fans he comes across as quite a quirky, interesting, left-field figure. The mantra he set out when he first arrived was quite counter-culturalist, to challenge the establishment, and that fits well here," Parker said.

"You will see him walking along on the seafront, going up for coffees around town and he travels back and forth on an ebike, not in a chauffer-driven car as a lot of managers might. He's also hosted fan events in pubs, which I believe he paid for. So I'd say he's very approachable."

But Hürzeler isn't the only 30-something German beloved in Brighton. Pascal Gross, who rejoined the club from Borussia Dortmund in January, is also a firm favorite. The midfielder, who retired from Germany duty after the World Cup earlier this year, has scored three and made four in the club's opening seven league games and said he felt compelled to return.
"I missed the special connection I have with the people here," the 35-year-old told Sky Sports.

blocks.caption: Pascal Gross has been a key player for Brighton since returning to the club in JanuaryImage: Richard Lee/Shutterstock/IMAGO

blocks.text: "I was here for seven years, got married here and both my kids were born in England. The most important milestones in my life happened here. I missed my friends and the feeling of being deeply connected to the club."

The feeling is mutual, said Parker. "Pascal Gross is everybody's favorite player. He's Brighton's first best signing, from Ingolstadt, and second-best signing, from Dortmund. He's a sensational player, and it's probably true to say there is a lot of warmth towards towards German football and Germany because of these hugely important characters at the football club."
Hürzeler has Bayern in mind, but Brighton in present

The Premier League club's success has been built on a smart coach and player recruitment strategy guided by local owner, Tony Bloom. Part of the model is that those who shine brightest will often be snatched by the bigger fish.

"I think he's said he's a supporter of Bayern Munich and he uses them as an example of the standards he wants," said Parker of Hürzeler. "I can see that he could be a good fit in a couple of years time. He won't go to a Liverpool or a Chelsea, I think there's a strong pull to Bayern in particular."

Bayern's current boss, Vincent Kompany, is in little danger at the moment, though Bayern coaches are only ever a few losses from crisis. For the meantime, Hürzeler is also happy where he is, having extended his contract to 2029. Again, the feeling is mutual.

Next up in the Premier League is a trip to Liverpool, where Jürgen Klopp became the first German coach to make a real mark on the Premier League. But before that, Hürzeler's team have an assignment in the Europa Conference League, a competition Brighton are among the favorites to win. Parker hopes a first major trophy is in sight.
"If he can be the person that wins us that first trophy, then he will go down as the greatest."
